Executive Summary 
What is the 15-Year T&D Electric Planning Report? 
The 2019 NY 15 Year Electric Transmission and Distribution (T&D) Planning Report (this 
“Plan”) is a long-range plan to help guide Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation d/b/a 
National Grid (“National Grid” or the “Company”) through the major changes and challenges 
expected over the next 15 years.  This Plan is founded on a core commitment to exceed 
customer expectations, to enable growth and prosperity in the communities we serve, and 
to make possible an affordable, sustainable, and secure energy system for tomorrow.  
Bringing this energy vision to life requires a proactive, customer-centered, mission-driven 
approach.   
Our approach begins with a focus on optimizing performance.  This is reflected in the 
Company’s commitment to always find a better way.  In this plan, we have identified 
foundational investments that will enable National Grid to modernize the grid, improve 
efficiency, animate markets, and enhance the reliability and resiliency of the electric system. 
With those threshold improvements in place, National Grid will also be well positioned to 
accelerate its efforts to “green” the grid.  By facilitating the interconnection of distributed 
and large-scale renewable generation and using innovative solutions to address challenges 
created by intermittent energy supplies, we believe we can make substantial progress 
toward meeting the State’s clean energy goals and the Company’s strategic vision. 
This Plan will be used to inform major decisions and investments on the T&D system during 
that time.  It is a “living document” that the Company will revise every two years to 
incorporate changes over time as the industry evolves.  In this Plan, National Grid provides 
an assessment of where it is today, where it will be tomorrow, as well as how it intends to 
get there.

Where are we Today? 
Today, National Grid primarily delivers electricity from third party generation resources 
through its T&D system to customers.  It is responsible for safely, reliably, and affordably 
delivering energy that fulfills customers’ needs. The Company promotes and facilitates new 
interconnection of loads and generation across the T&D system, including interconnecting 
an increasing amount of distributed energy resources (DER), while maintaining reliability.  
The Company also works closely with the New York State Independent System Operator 
(NYISO) and other industry stakeholders to ensure the T&D system maintains its reliability 
as some large-scale generation retirements occur and as new large-scale renewable (LSR) 
generation is added to the power system.  The Company is actively transitioning into an 
expanded role as the Distributed System Platform (DSP) provider and is developing projects 
to implement ambitious grid modernization goals of National Grid’s Electric Business Unit, 
in alignment with the goals set forth in the Commission’s Reforming the Energy Vision (REV) 
proceeding.  
Where are we Going Tomorrow? 
National Grid is putting to work the tools, skills, experience, and knowledge needed to help 
modernize the electrical power system and transform it to a cleaner, more efficient, 
decentralized, transactive, resilient, and sustainable grid of tomorrow.  Looking to the future, 
the electric power system will likely become a more accessible and agile platform that allows 
customers and other participants to interact and conduct energy transactions. This Plan is 
“Our purpose, which sets out why National Grid exists, is simple – we bring 
energy to life.” 
Our Vision: “We will exceed the expectations of our customers, 
shareholders, and communities today and make possible the energy 
systems of tomorrow.” 
Our Values: “Every day we do the right thing and find a better way”

aligned with that direction, and fully supports the clean-energy goals set forth in the State 
Energy Plan and the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act of 2019 (CLCPA). 
 
To avoid the most dire effects of climate change, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in 
developed countries must fall by at least 80 percent below 1990 levels by 2050.1  The CLCPA 
sets even more ambitious goals for the State of New York: reductions of GHG emissions from 
1990 levels of 40 percent by 2030 and 85 percent by 2050.  The Company has also recently 
announced its own ambitious target of achieving net-zero for its own emissions by 2050.   
Achieving decarbonization goals in our operating regions will require action across the three 
dominant 
sectors of combustion-related CO2 emissions: electricity generation, 
transportation, and heat.  Importantly, the emissions reductions realized to date relied 
largely on shifts in the electricity generation fuel mix. In contrast, the reductions required 
from here to 2030 and 2050 become far more personal. The clean energy transition begins 
with the electric generation sector, but by necessity moves beyond this and requires 
modifications to individual behaviors and choices in transportation and how we heat our 
homes and businesses.  
To increase grid efficiency, National Grid has been scaling up several programs, and will 
continue to expand customer-side energy efficiency (EE) and demand response (DR) 
programs, along with interconnecting and integrating increasing volumes of 3rd party-
deployed and customer-owned DER solutions. The Company is exploring and honing 
advanced planning techniques to help identify optimal locations for renewable generation, 
transmission corridors, and energy storage to “green” the grid.  The grid of the future not 
only maintains reliability but also enhances resiliency.  National Grid plans to build the grid 
of tomorrow by adding more sensors, communications, and software that support highly 
granular data analytics, advanced planning, and autonomous grid operation.  Building a grid 
that is resilient and will also enable efficient energy use and transactions among system 
participants will require a healthy wire-based foundation.  By utilizing advanced planning 
and targeting deployment of various technologies, the Company anticipates program and 
system improvements will occur.  These improvements will lead to optimized investments 
and maximizing the benefit to customers.  In this Plan, National Grid sets forth its vision for 
tomorrow’s grid.

How are we Going to Get There? 
There will be challenges along the road to developing the grid of the future.  This Plan 
discusses many of those challenges along with potential solutions and opportunities for 
customers.  
Some of the challenges include: 
➢ Bringing efficiencies to a grid that has evolved over decades and is comprised of 
multiple generations of technology with different integration capabilities; 
➢ Transitioning from a grid that provides power in a single direction to a transactive 
grid with bi-directional power flows and complex value-based secure market 
transactions; 
➢ Moving toward a more decentralized system and increasing the delivery of clean-
energy supplies; 
➢ Integrating non-traditional solutions, including through NWAs, at a reasonable cost; 
➢ Efficiently integrating third-party resources; 
➢ Maintaining the reliability of an increasingly complex grid built on aging 
infrastructure; 
➢ Continuing to enhance resiliency in the face of climate change and grid adjustments; 
and 
➢ Cybersecurity. 
 
The status quo – business as usual – is not an option to fulfill the demands of the future.  We 
embrace the change, and are committed to working with customers, regulators, and other 
stakeholders to find a better way to bring a new energy future to life. In this Plan, the 
Company provides a detailed roadmap outlining its approach for overcoming some of these 
challenges.  The roadmap covers two specific periods, 0-5 years and 6-15 years, and defines 
how National Grid plans to build the grid of tomorrow.

Chapter 1: Introduction 
 
The energy sector is undergoing transformation.  It faces greater change and uncertainty 
than ever before, which brings fresh challenges and new opportunities.  In light of these 
changes, National Grid has developed this Plan as a long-range guide to inform the 
Company’s decision-making over the next 15 years.  This Plan will be revised every two years 
and is a “living document” that will change as the industry evolves.  This Plan assesses where 
the grid needs to be tomorrow and how the Company plans to get there. The Plan is 
organized within the context of National Grid’s overarching Purpose, Vision, and Values to 
form the main four chapters (Grid Efficiency, Market Animation, Greening the Grid, and Grid 
Resiliency). The Plan then presents a customer-focused roadmap identifying actions within 
these four themes that the Company will work to implement over the next 15 years.  The 
final chapter of the Plan presents “Topic Papers” focused on specific key areas which will be 
critical to the continued successful modernization, “greening,” and safe and reliable 
operation of the grid to effectively fulfill customer’s needs.  
Our purpose 
Having a clear sense of what the Company stands for 
and what binds us all together is vitally important. 
This is what National Grid calls its purpose. In simple 
terms, it is what drives the Company to serve 
customers and it is the thing that makes National 
Grid’s employees proud of the work they do. 
Our purpose is to bring energy to life.  In its simplest 
form, “bring energy to life” means getting the heat, 
light and power that customers rely on to their homes 
and businesses.  But “life” also means supporting the 
communities that we are a part of and live in, as well 
as supporting the economic growth and sustainability 
of wider society. 
Our vision 
Our vision describes how National Grid creates value – not just today, but in the future too. 
The needs of customers, shareholders and communities are at the heart of everything 
National Grid does. Our vision describes this ambitious approach – to make sure the 
Company delivers value for these constituencies every day.

Chapter 2: Grid Efficiency 
 
2.1 Challenges and Opportunities 
The modern electric grid is a product of over 100 years of evolution; to this day it continues 
to operate using some of its earliest infrastructure.  This poses significant challenges for 
electric utilities. For instance, electric T&D system losses across the United States are just 
under 5 percent of the total energy delivered.2  Although this may seem like a relatively small 
percentage, it represents a substantial loss of energy when considering the sheer volume of 
energy delivered. Perhaps an even greater challenge for the industry is to increase grid 
utilization factors by identifying ways to make better use of the assets already in place.  For 
example, utilities traditionally have engineered the grid to be capable of serving peak loads 
(accounting for potential contingency events) that may occur only a few hours each year.  
This provides very high reliability, but can have low utilization factors and can result in 
higher costs for customers.   
Reducing peak demand to avoid or defer wholesale generation capacity and T&D peak 
capacity investments was a core focus of the REV proceeding.  Likewise, the Company is 
committed to pursuing ways to economically reduce system power losses, increase 
efficiencies, and make full use of DER when possible.  To do this, the Company needs to better 
understand where, why, and how system energy losses occur. Such information is important 
to developing cost-effective solutions with broad benefits.  Recent improvements in 
communications technologies, monitoring equipment, and computing capabilities will 
enable the Company to deliver energy more efficiently by optimizing how the T&D system 
operates.  Indeed, the ability to collect a wide variety of field measurements and transmit 
that information in real time to high-speed centralized control systems has opened new 
opportunities for “tuning” the grid and optimizing the way customers use energy. Advanced 
Metering Infrastructure (AMI) is a core component of the Company’s vision that will enable 
customers to take meaningful action to conserve energy and manage their energy costs.       
The Company has already started the journey toward grid efficiency, with DR and EE 
programs becoming core business areas.  In addition, demonstration projects such as the 
Company’s partnership in Clifton Park, New York, to deploy Volt-VAR Optimization (VVO) 
technology, are providing valuable insights into technical capabilities and optimal 
approaches for future system design. The REV demonstration project included the 
implementation of VVO on 11 feeders split between two substations. The VVO schemes 
became operational in April 2019 and are undergoing functionality testing as the project 
engages in a Measurement and Verification process through March 2020.

2.2 Objectives 
The Company has three grid-efficiency objectives: increasing T&D efficiency in New York, 
creating new markets to drive EE, and reducing energy costs. These objectives align with 
New York’s overarching clean energy goals.

The Company will identify areas where it will deploy grid efficiency-related programs within 
the three core initiatives in a targeted manner that benefits customers and the grid.  For 
example, using NWA and rates developed through New York’s Value of Distributed Energy 
Resources (VDER) proceeding, the Company fosters DER deployment in areas that can lead 
to deferred or avoided investments in wholesale generation capacity and T&D peak capacity, 
while simultaneously reducing T&D system losses. Similarly, the DR program should 
increasingly focus on areas that require load relief. It is worth noting, building on these 
programs by utilizing modern technology represents a shift in the industry that will require 
continued innovation and focus.  At the same time,  the Company will continue to take 
advantage of more traditional resources to increase efficiency, such as converting to higher 
transmission and distribution voltages and adding Conservation Voltage Reduction (CVR) 
devices strategically, where economically beneficial for customers.  
To enable these programs to flourish and provide customer benefits, the Company will likely 
need to increase investments in a suite of technologies that can support multiple programs 
simultaneously, including: 
• High-speed communications 
• Integrated advanced controls 
• Line sensors 
• AMI with grid-side benefits 
• Advanced Distribution Management System (ADMS) 
• Distributed Energy Resource Management System (DERMS) 
• Next generation consumer appliances and systems (e.g., HVAC) 
• Energy storage systems (ESS) 
For example, DERMS is vital to the management and control of distributed assets and DERs, 
making it key to optimizing grid efficiency.  AMI, which will provide real-time data on 
customer use, is also key. The more rapidly these foundational technologies are deployed, 
the quicker the Company can deliver a more efficient grid with more accurate, granular price 
signals for its customers.

Focus on Customer – Greenpac Mill’s leadership team recently set two ambitious goals—create 100 percent beneficial waste 
by the end of 2020 and reduce energy consumption by five percent by the end of 2019. In addition to recycling 2,000 tons of 
cardboard per day, the linerboard manufacturer separates other waste materials, such as plastics, secondary fibers and metals, 
and delivers them to other local companies and organizations. Greenpac Mill’s first capital expense was to change all the 
interior and exterior lights to LED. National Grid offered over $500,000 of incentives to Greenpac for this investment. Not only 
did Greenpac Mill pay $0.00 for the upgrade to LED bulbs, the plant also saved over $175,000 in annual energy costs. 
To provide choice and value to customers, the Company identified Sub-Programs within the 
three core grid-efficiency initiatives outlined above.  For example, the DR Program includes 
the Distribution Load Relief Program (DLRP) and the Commercial System Relief Program 
(CSRP), among others.  As shown in the figure below, the success of the various grid-
efficiency programs and the Company’s corresponding ability to meet its grid-efficiency 
objectives is premised on investing in foundational technologies.  More details of the grid-
efficiency programs associated technologies can be found in the Chapter 7 Topic Catalog.

Consistent with its Distributed System Implementation Plan (DSIP), the Company expects 
that the earliest and largest investments in support of customer adoption of DER and 
increased control over energy consumption to be in AMI and grid modernization 
(distribution automation, telecommunications and control center systems).  The Company 
further expects investments in cyber security and operational systems (such as EMS, ADMS, 
and DERMS) will follow to support the grid-efficiency objectives.  As two of the three 
Programs interface directly with the customer, cyber security and privacy are vital and will 
continue to be interlaced throughout deployment. 
The Company’s targeted approach to grid efficiency aligns with the goal of creating expanded 
and animated markets stimulated by incentives derived from geospatial and temporal 
dispatch of decentralized assets. The Company anticipates that grid-efficiency programs will 
likely evolve with DSP developments, starting as managed programs that become more 
autonomous. This approach should help to create an optimized grid, expanding utilization of 
existing assets while also increasing use of DERs. Real-time asset visibility, such as that 
provided by AMI with grid-side benefits, is a necessary precursor to an optimized grid.

Non-Wires Alternatives  
 
NWA adds non-traditional solutions to the Company’s planning tool box. For example, with 
NWA performance contracts, the Company may defer or avoid the need for traditional wires-
based projects.  Each NWA is assessed through a Benefit-Cost Analysis (BCA) that captures 
multiple value streams, such as the environmental improvements and avoided wholesale 
costs.  Only those NWA solutions that demonstrate a sufficiently positive BCA result will be 
selected to ensure the highest value to National Grid’s customers.  Common NWA 
technologies include, but are not limited to: Dynamic Load Management (DLM), Distributed 
Generation (DG), EE, and ESS.

DERs:

from an RFP-based approach to a value-based retail DSP market.

Chapter 3: Market Animation 
 
3.1 Challenges and Opportunities 
There are many factors driving load customers’ and DER developers’ desire to play a greater 
role regarding how, where, and when energy is consumed and generated. For example, load 
customers want greater awareness of their energy consumption and options available to 
reduce, modify, self-supply, and procure energy. DER developers seek new value streams 
and opportunities to grow their DER portfolios, such as new market products akin to the 
wholesale NYISO market.  It is National Grid’s role as the DSP to integrate all participants 
into a marketplace that fosters a more reliable, sustainable, flexible, value-driven, open, 
competitive, fair, secure, and cost-effective distribution system and that helps to achieve the 
State’s energy goals. The figures below illustrate the utility’s role as the DSP described in the

Long-Term Goals for DSP Functions within Each Core DSP Service Area 
In today’s retail market, the value of electricity is not accurately reflected in customer bills.  
For example, the wholesale price of electricity varies over time and geography however, the 
vast majority of retail customers are generally charged a flat monthly commodity billing rate 
irrespective of when and where electricity is consumed.  Similarly, as some customers 
become “prosumers” utilizing DERs, historical payment structures have not accurately 
reflected the costs or benefits of their impact on the grid. To address this, electricity markets 
are evolving to accommodate all participants and fairly compensate them for value they 
provide to the grid and/or charge them based on the costs they place on the grid. New market 
products are emerging along with the processes and tools to facilitate them.   
Prior to NY-REV initiative, there was limited coupling/interaction between distribution 
tariffs/programs and wholesale markets.  For example: 
• Averaged flat cost distribution of NYISO wholesale LSE (Load Serving Entity) 
procurements and grid infrastructure costs for all residential customers. 
• Net energy metering based only on reduction in customer bills at retail rates. 
• Limited NYISO DR participation. 
• TOU rates for large C&I customers only. 
• Demand charges that did not directly align with grid needs. 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 502 of 1030


--- Page 22 ---
Page 21 of 317 
 
Today’s market structure, referred to as the DSP 1.0 in the 2018 DSIP 5 Year update report, 
provides greater grid interaction and supports increased market participation and activity.  
For example, DSP 1.0 promotes increased DER integration up to the limitations of today’s 
distribution grid. Utilities have sufficient visibility and operational control over large DER 
to maintain safe and reliable grid operations. Operational coordination with the NYISO is 
based on pre-determined rules for joint participation in NWA procurements and the NYISO 
markets.  Under today’s structure, there is greater coupling of programs, markets and rates 
with distribution system, and the NYISO wholesale market.  For example, VDER (NEM 
successor) now incorporates a window of need for distribution capacity relief termed LSRV 
(Locational Specific Relief Value), and energy and capacity wholesale market value. Also, 
expanded DR programs capture system wide value into participation payments.  Further 
market evolution will result in increased instances of: 
• NWAs paying DER developers to meet local grid needs. 
• Targeted DR programs directly supporting local grid needs. 
• Integration with future NYISO DER markets4. 
• TOU rates for all customers with AMI5. 
The DSP 2.0 market structure will build on the functions and capabilities of DSP 1.0 as DER 
technology and energy management software platforms evolve (e.g., DERMS) and the costs 
of communications reduce, adding significantly greater visibility and operational control 
over large and aggregations of small DER as shown in the figure below.  Greater visibility and 
operational control will allow for the creation of integrated markets and operation for 
wholesale and distribution services. In DSP 2.0, DSPs will offer wholesale scheduling and 
dispatch services, allowing customers and aggregators to maximize the value of their 
resources across NYISO wholesale markets and distribution markets. Aggregators and 
customers will still be able to access wholesale markets directly through the NYISO. The DSP 
and NYISO will have enhanced capabilities to monitor and control DER.

DSP 1.0-2.3 Development and Enabling Elements 
 
The Company recently completed a DSP demonstration project that developed and tested a 
dynamically varying and NYISO linked pricing stack at the Buffalo Niagara Medical Campus.  
That demonstration provided many useful lessons and the development of a software tool 
that the Company plans to build and continue investigating the developments of DSP 
markets such as: 
• Peer to Peer Hosting Capacity Market – National Grid’s current 15-year forecast6 
shows the significant impact of an approximately 1 GW drop to the minimum load in 
2033 from today due to solar PV.  Without load to support this level of solar PV, there 
could be significant impacts on the local distribution system from high voltages and 
thermal limits due to back-feeding. Programs, markets, or rates that encourage 
mitigation measures (e.g., “negative DR” or “flexible load”), during such periods could 
help offset significant expenditures in distribution and potentially transmission 
system upgrades needed to accommodate high levels of solar PV.  New and growing 
technologies like EVs, storage, and other flexible load sources such as heat pumps 
could participate in such a program.  National Grid, as the DSP, would facilitate the 
peer to peer market transactions between operators of the PV facilities and the 
flexible load resources.

• Reliability Market - Some areas are seeing concentrated load growth where the 
increased load is causing feeder tie constraints and raising risk exposure. A DSP 
market with prices based on value of $/CMI (Customer Minutes Interrupted) could 
target locations where DER can reduce unfaulted feeder section loading, allowing a 
greater level of load transfer from the faulted feeder.   
• Peer to Peer Community Resiliency Market – “Resiliency” has become an 
increasingly crucial component for the grid of the future considering potential climate 
change impacts. There are many traditional solutions to building a more resilient grid 
such as undergrounding overhead lines, stronger poles and wires, and substation 
storm hardening. However, as more DER integrates into the grid, DER-supplied 
microgrids present another potential solution to improve grid resiliency. New 
programs, markets, or rates, akin to the NYISO black start market, that appropriately 
value resiliency could incentivize novel solutions to grid resiliency through services 
provided by DER. 
Other considerations, such as better prediction of local and NYISO peak load hours, increased 
integration between distribution price signals and the NYISO Real Time Market, reactive 
power markets, and moving towards the development of the DSP as the balancing authority, 
could all increase the value provided by DERs and the platform value of the DSPs.

number of market animation-related topics that National Grid is currently working to fulfill.

Electric Vehicle (EV) Sub-program Example 
As described in the EV topic section of this Plan, the Company has identified two potential 
scenarios: Percent of New Registrations (PNR), and ZEV (Zero Emission Vehicle) 
Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) target. While the ZEV scenario is expected to have 
the greatest level of growth, either scenario is expected to have a significant impact on the 
grid.  This EV growth is partially derived by the effect of ongoing price reductions in EVs 
combined with a  NYSERDA state rebate of $2,000 and a federal tax credit of between $2,500 
to $7,500 per new EV purchased for use in the U.S. The size of the tax credit depends on the

size of the vehicle and its battery capacity.7  NYSERDA also offers incentives for public

With an expected significant increase in electrical load from EVs over the 15-year horizon, 
three major components are likely required for EVs to flourish and enable the State’s goal of 
40 percent reduction in GHG emissions by 2030: 
1. Strengthening the grid in areas with high penetrations of forecasted EVs to be 
identified via advanced forecasting and granular modeling; 
2. Managed EV charging via TOU market-based pricing or other pricing signals that 
encourage customized charging patterns for EV customers (or groups of customers) 
to alleviate grid overloading, help integrate renewable generation by aligning load 
with renewable generation and simultaneously providing customer choice over 
utility control;9 and 
3. Continuing to advance the build out of EV charging infrastructure.10 
National Grid has already made significant inroads in these three areas as described in more 
detail in the EV topic section of the Plan.

Chapter 4: Greening the Grid 
 
4.1 Challenges and Opportunities 
The traditional configuration of the electric grid utilizes large conventional generators 
connected almost exclusively to the transmission system with power flowing to customers 
in one direction.  However, this arrangement is rapidly changing as renewable generation 
sources permeate the electric system and produce bi-directional power flows.  
Approximately 29 percent of New York’s electrical energy was generated from renewable 
sources in 2018.12  With the goals set out by National Grid and the CLCPA targets requiring 
70 percent of energy be produced from renewable resources by the year 2030, the challenge 
to increase the amount of interconnected renewable energy sources at both the T&D levels 
of the grid is significant.  This will require continued system modifications to assure safe and 
reliable operation for National Grid’s customers. The Company is committed to enabling this 
transformation.  Our solutions are and will continue to be strategically targeted at 
overcoming challenges of greening the grid, specifically: interconnection and siting, system 
integration, and cost-effective procurement. 
The Company has implemented meaningful improvements to its DG interconnection process 
and will continue to proactively improve this process to enable renewables on the system.  
The location to construct renewable generation has not always aligned with locations that 
would be most beneficial for T&D system needs.  High-load areas near towns and cities tend 
to have insufficient land available for solar or wind installations, as well as higher costs to 
purchase and develop the land that is available. As a result, comparatively inexpensive and 
undeveloped rural locations maybe more attractive to developers for solar and wind 
installations.  While these areas may present lower development costs, they often present 
challenges for the rural electric system, which is designed for a sparsely populated area with 
low electrical demand.  In short, these areas typically have smaller substations and long 
radial distribution lines that may not be well suited for DG interconnections. As a result, 
interconnecting renewable generation on rural feeders may require substantial 
infrastructure upgrades to facilitate the comparatively large power flow onto the system and 
may make the location cost prohibitive. New tariff structures such as the Value Stack, and 
more specifically the LSRV component of the Value Stack, is one step towards encouraging 
interconnections in mutually beneficial locations. Hosting capacity analysis and the 
associated results have been another step in the right direction. 
Similarly, LSR installations connected to the transmission system often encounter 
comparable challenges.  These facilities tend to be proposed in locations where the 
respective resource (e.g., wind, solar) is optimal and land (or locations off-shore in the case 
of wind generation) is available; such locations, however, are typically not near high-load 
areas.  Interconnecting those resources may require additional transmission lines, 
                                                          
12 See U.S. Energy Information Association, New York State Profile and Energy Estimates, available at 
https://www.eia.gov/state/index.php?sid=NY (last visited Oct. 29, 2019). 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 515 of 1030


--- Page 35 ---
Page 34 of 317 
 
specialized cables, and high-voltage substations to transmit the energy generated to load 
areas.  By addressing these challenges, the Company will be able to work with its customers 
and third parties to facilitate the optimal flow of renewable generation to urban centers 
while supporting the State Energy Plan and furthering clean energy goals.  
Constructing additional renewable generation sources and interconnecting them to the grid 
represents only the first step.  The ability of the grid to effectively utilize the energy produced 
from renewable sources also needs to be carefully considered.  Wind, solar, and hydro (to 
some extent) energy sources are intermittent and do not always generate coincident with 
energy needs.  This intermittency presents an operational challenge, as it is contrary to the 
typical situation, where generation must match demand at all times to maintain grid stability.  
To complicate this challenge, several base load generation units in New York could retire by 
2030, the largest being 2 GW of nuclear power generated at the Indian Point Energy Center.13  
If the retirements occur, New York would lose approximately 12 percent14 of the State’s base 
load generation, further increasing the risk of generation-to-demand imbalances.   
The technology used to interconnect renewable generation sources differs significantly from 
the traditional synchronous generation currently used to produce the majority of energy on 
the grid.  Renewable generation sources are predominantly inverter-connected, or 
asynchronous (induction) machines.  This presents challenges with respect to system inertia 
(stability), as well as power quality, and requires careful consideration to maintain safe and 
reliable operation of the electric system.  These issues are presently addressed using large 
synchronous generators, enabling the interconnection of the existing classes of renewable 
resources.  
 Although the loss of synchronous machines and system inertia is not expected to be a major 
issue in the short term, it is an important consideration for long-term planning.  Strategies 
need to be considered to proactively prepare for a larger percentage of inverter-connected 
generation sources with significantly increased capacity.  The Company included initial 
short-term strategies to improve system stability in recent interconnection standards 
updates.  Other strategies for consideration include utilizing an inverter’s capability to 
control steady-state reactive power to improve efficiency and power factor.  Additionally, 
the pairing of synchronous condensers with larger renewable generators may be a viable 
option to provide the necessary system inertia.  While synchronous condensers were used 
previously at many large industrial plants in the early 20th century (e.g., at steel plants with 
electric arc furnaces), their use became less necessary as generation stations grew larger and 
grids became more interconnected. 
Over the past several years there has been a proliferation of LSR generation across New York.  
However, as some subsidies begin to phase out, there could be a significant decline in 
requests to interconnect such generation to the system and/or increases in the cost of 
                                                          
13 U.S. Energy Information Administration, Indian Point, closest nuclear plant to New York City, set to retire by 2021, 
available at https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=29772. 
14 Id.

Page 35 of 317 
 
renewable energy credits.15  This, in turn, would make it even more challenging to reach the 
70 percent renewable generation by 2030 goal.  To overcome that challenge, the Company 
will continue to evaluate and support initiatives aimed at developing LSR capacity, including 
(with regulatory authorization) potential opportunities for utility-owned LSR as a least-cost 
option for customers. 
Potential measures to manage the effects of base load generation loss and the significant 
increase in renewable generation include the following:   
➢ Canadian Hydro and a new Transmission Highway16  
The project would allow for the transmission of renewable energy to distant load 
centers. Permitting new transmission lines can be challenging and time consuming. 
However, new transmission with new large-scale resources offers substantial 
benefits in achieving the State’s clean energy targets. 
➢ Demand Response and Energy Efficiency  
Enable the ability to control load demand in line with system capabilities.  While DR 
and EE will be important tools in helping match load to production, they cannot 
completely replace generation, as the majority of the Company’s customers will 
continue to call on energy supplies to meet their preferred schedules. 
➢ Energy Storage Systems  
ESS is often seen as a key component to renewable generation integration due to its 
ability to resolve challenges that confront the grid when interconnecting renewable 
generation.  For example, ESS can alleviate renewable interconnection limitations 
often reflected in the so-called “duck curve,”17 where a large supply of variable 
generation reduces mid-day demand but gives way to a steep ramp up of non-variable 
generation later in the day as variable sources cease producing.  ESS can also address 
challenges created by the intermittency of renewable supplies.  The ability to smooth 
the intermittent power gaps caused by renewable energy sources and optimize 
power flows along feeders and substation equipment is highly desirable.  ESS is 
rapidly evolving technologically and it appears to follow a similar cost trajectory to 
solar (see figure below showing solar PV cell cost reduction against production 
capacity from 1976 to 2014 and Lithium-ion battery cost reductions from 2010 for 
Electric Vehicles). While ESS is not necessarily a new technology, with approximately 
1.5 GW of pumped hydro storage18 currently operating in New York (primarily the 
Blenheim Gilboa and Lewiston plants), other forms of ESS such as batteries, thermal, 
and compressed air are considered new. These systems will act as both a load and a 
source, and therefore require careful analysis.

National Grid has made significant progress in the field of Energy Storage recently,

will have to continue to meet our Green Goals. 
The Company expects the overall solution will require a mix of all the approaches listed 
above.  For example, renewable DG paired with DR and ESS can bring additional benefits, 
such as reduced T&D congestion and losses by supplying energy close to, or within, load 
pockets and even providing additional resiliency throughout the smart grid.  Pairing these 
new technologies enables the Company to construct a more efficient and reliable system 
while improving the environment for National Grid’s customers.

4.3 Plan 
Over the next 15 years, the Company will play a major role in greening the grid, by 
considering opportunities to deploy LSR generation, facilitating T&D renewable generation 
interconnections, and maintaining a stable grid.  To do this the Company will focus on three 
major programs/initiatives: 
 
The Company will consider owning utility-scale LSR through a model that favors merchant 
developers and customers titled “Build-Own-Transfer.”  Within an appropriate framework, 
this model leverages renewable energy developers’ expertise and provides significant 
customer savings through performance-based cost-of-service rates. The Company will 
continue to evaluate and monitor the cost to customers through available local and national 
finance models.  
The Company also plays a key role in the interconnection of renewable generation at the 
T&D level.  This is achieved primarily through interconnection studies, system upgrade 
identification, and installing wire-based interconnection assets.21  Meeting the 70 percent 
target requires approximately six times22 the amount of renewable generating capacity 
presently installed.  To help address this gap, the Company has invested in DG 
interconnection tools that capture the latest standards and can conduct interconnection 
studies faster.  These tools screen analyses and results to help engineers focus their time on 
pertinent questions that require engineering judgment to ensure safe and reliable 
interconnections. For example, in 2017, the Company introduced the Interconnection Online 
Application Portal (IOAP) that accelerates and simplifies DG interconnections for National 
Grid’s customers, with Phase 2 going live in 2019.  Furthermore, hosting capacity maps are 
available to direct customers to areas that have lower DG interconnection costs.  See figures 
below.

interconnection. In addition, the Company will continue to identify and propose 
transmission solutions to transmission constraints that could interfere with the

appropriate.  
For the foregoing reasons, the Company also sees a major role for ESS in the grid of the 
future.23  An ESS demonstration project is currently operational in New York at the East 
Pulaski substation.  The purpose of the project is to alleviate a supply constraint and an “N-
1” distribution constraint, respectively.  Similarly, NWA proposals often include ESS as the 
technology of choice, especially for reliability issues.  In fact, the Company is planning to 
procure dispatch rights of between 10MW and 50MW+ of ESS to meet several planning needs 
(deferring and/or eliminating the need for potential traditional investments in those 
locations), while also participating in NYISO wholesale energy and ancillary services 
markets. The Company plans to use lessons learned from these projects to increase 
engineers’ experience and confidence using ESS as a new planning and operations tool that 
benefits the system and customers.  The Company will continue to work closely with NY 
BEST (technology developments and testing), NYSERDA (Clean Energy Fund), and interested 
stakeholders to enable successful integration of ESS technologies.

Probabilistic Forecasts 
Combining the benefits of ESS with local DG and smart grid technologies can also provide the 
opportunity to increase resiliency by creating microgrids. The Company plans to explore 
working in partnership with developers and customers to build microgrids that benefit all 
stakeholders. Lessons learned from NYSERDA’s NY Prize competition and the Potsdam 
demonstration project will inform possible future microgrid developments.  
As the Company evaluates these technologies and opportunities over the next 15 years, the 
grid will become more complex.  To address the challenges created by that complexity, while 
also creating benefits for the system and customers, the Company is developing a new “One 
System – One Model” approach to system planning.  This new approach will facilitate 
advanced planning that integrates NYISO transmission models with sub-transmission, 
distribution, DERs, and customer loads.  This will be a significant undertaking, starting with 
the Company’s current effort to build a bottom-up model of the grid using a cloud-based 
software platform that greatly enhances modeling, simulation, and analysis capabilities.  
The One System – One Model approach will incorporate various probabilistic forecasts and 
provide the ability to overlap and integrate multiple layers of data.  These capabilities will 
help enable various study tools to access the same model every time and allow the Company 
to identify targeted opportunities to green the grid.  As part the Company’s VDER modeling 
effort, NYISO models are currently being expanded to include more granular sub-
transmission & distribution station information. These expanded models will tie feeder-level 
data up to the transmission level to enable more advanced analysis of the grid.

Chapter 5: Resilient Grid 
 
5.1 Challenges and Opportunities 
The Company strives to maintain its assets and networks to the criteria under which they 
were built.  But most of the system was not designed to withstand today’s climate and still 
meet reliability demands. The frequency and severity of extreme weather events are 
increasing. Between March and May 2018 there were five events in NY that impacted over 
100,000 customers. The increasing frequency and severity of these events adversely affects 
customers and drives increased costs.   
Despite the growing concern over the critical need for enhanced electric system resiliency, 
there is no standardized framework for assessing system weaknesses and benefits. While 
high-impact, low-frequency events are not preventable, the primary goal of a resiliency 
strategy is to limit the impacts on customers and communities. National Grid’s transmission 
system would be planned to address EPRI’s definitions and tactics to improve transmission 
system storm resiliency.25 The EPRI resiliency definition is divided into three components: 
(1) Damage Prevention; (2) System Recovery; and (3) Survivability. There are many factors 
that the Company is considering while evaluating these core resiliency components, such as 
population density and geography.  
The Company’s service territory is diverse, ranging from congested urban areas with densely 
populated city environments to ultra-rural areas like the heavily forested Adirondacks with 
its tree-trimming restrictions.  Each area presents its own challenges and opportunities with 
regard to resiliency.  Underground networks and high-voltage cables in cities are largely 
insulated from storm impacts.  Conversely, long overhead distribution and transmission 
circuits with minimal loads in rural areas require the Company to proactively design the 
system to withstand weather-related impacts like heavy ice loading and wind.  
Despite the geographic breadth of the Company’s service territory, National Grid’s electric 
system has proven reliable.  National Grid has also designed and built resiliency into the 
system.  For example, the design of the networked distribution system in downtown Buffalo 
enabled the City to form a regional “island” in August 2003 and avoid the worst effects of the 
Northeast blackout.  
In other areas of the Company’s service territory, resiliency is more challenging.  Sparsely 
populated rural areas, for example, are served by long overhead lines.  These long lines 
remain exposed to, among other things, falling trees, lightning, storm damage, and motor 
vehicle accidents.  While National Grid builds resilience into its basic designs and 
infrastructure, it is often difficult and expensive to create a system that can withstand 
adversity under all conditions.  National Grid seeks to determine if there is a better way to 
reduce the costs and increase the benefits of building a more resilient electric grid.  To do 
this, the Company has partnered with like-minded customers, including the Potsdam 
                                                          
25 See https://www.naseo.org/Data/Sites/1/resiliency-white-paper.pdf 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 526 of 1030


--- Page 46 ---
Page 45 of 317 
 
government, businesses, and universities, to investigate resilient technology, including 
smart grids and microgrids in Potsdam. 
The Potsdam Microgrid project26 explored microgrid applications in a rural setting in 
northern New York. The project puts customers at the center, with participants such as  
Clarkson University, SUNY Potsdam, Village offices, first responders like the local police and 
fire departments, waste and potable water treatment facilities, the hospital, and other 
important local services such as fuel, lodging, and pharmacies. It concentrates on servicing 
the local population needs to get through an extreme weather event or other emergency 
while National Grid works to restore the power system as quickly as possible. National Grid 
performed an in-depth techno-economic analysis of the Potsdam area to inform a design for 
the microgrid. The analysis also looked into the economics of the proposed microgrid, not 
just forecasting costs to build, but exploring various recovery models based on customer 
benefits. Lessons learned are discussed further in the Microgrid section in Chapter 7.  
The Company expects to continue evaluating microgrid opportunities beyond 
demonstration projects as additional customer groups seek to explore microgrid benefits.  
The Company is actively exploring microgrid opportunities in areas of the system where 
alternative reliability upgrades are infeasible (based on cost or technical restrictions). 
National Grid has found that areas served by a single (radial), relatively long transmission or 
sub-transmission source can be ideal locations to locate microgrids (since building a second 
source may be infeasibly costly). In fact, National Grid has released an RFP27 which aims to 
procure a 20MW/40MWh ESS specifically for this purpose; islanding a portion of the radial 
sub-transmission in the event of an upstream outage. More opportunities like this are being 
actively explored now and can be expected to present themselves over the next 15 years.  
In response to the increased frequency and intensity of storms, the Company continually 
seeks to improve its crisis preparedness and response plans.  This includes ensuring that 
emergency services have the power they need to serve local communities during critical 
incidents.  
In Response to Case 19-E-0110 – Proceeding on Motion of the Commission Investigating 
Utility Preparation and Response to Power Outages During the 2018 Winter and Spring 
Storms, Recommendation No. 88, the Company stated that it had reviewed its 115kV system 
to identify locations where transmission upgrades could result in an improvement to storm 
related outages (i.e. Survivability).  
The initial identification of customer risk was performed by reviewing single supply stations 
that serve over 5,000 customers, areas where loss of a single transmission line would 
interrupt over 10,000 customers, and areas where loss of two circuits would interrupt over 
20,000 customers. To address the customer risks, National Grid plans to invest in numerous 
transmission projects that are meant to minimize the number of customer outages that

would be exposed to a loss of a single line element or minimize outage duration by improved 
detection and fault isolation capabilities. In addition to minimizing exposure, National Grid 
must consider how it responds to storm events that cause customer outages. 
One of National Grid’s biggest challenges when responding during major storms is 
mobilization.  Such events may involve heavy damage from fallen trees that can take down 
overhead power distribution and sub-transmission systems.  Restoring power under these 
conditions is complicated, as tree damage and other storm conditions can make it difficult to 
move equipment into the affected areas.  To decrease the frequency of outages and mitigate 
the challenges of having to respond to outages, the Company has implemented improvement 
programs to “harden” the electric grid.  These efforts include a proactive tree-trimming 
program, recloser installations, and distribution standards to harden critical equipment 
installations.  The Company has also worked closely with communities to identify critical 
customers such as hospitals and to ensure effective communication with first responders 
during outage events.  More can always be done, which is why the Company is continuing to 
work with communities to identify cost-effective opportunities to improve grid resilience.   
Smart grid technologies will likely play a key role in the future of grid resiliency.  The 
Company believes opportunities exist beyond adding such technologies to existing wires-
based grid assets (e.g., adding communications and sensors to existing conductors, switches, 
regulators, and capacitor banks).  Therefore, to “harden” the electric grid and protect 
essential services, the Company will seek opportunities where it can combine grid 
modernization efforts that replace traditional assets with the installation of smart grid 
technologies. 
Although there are resiliency benefits to deploying smart grid technologies, great care must 
be taken to avoid exposing the grid to increased threats. This threat is more relevant than 
ever, with the first ever US electric grid cyber-attack occurring on March 5th 2019 to a 
Western US utility, reportedly temporarily disabling their SCADA system which control 
centers use to get real time grid data28.  
Leveraging a cyber secure smart grid with increasing opportunities to utilize customer and 
third-party-owned DER along with asset replacements is likely to bring cost-effective 
opportunities to efficiently increase grid resiliency.

5.2 Objectives 
National Grid has three objectives for continuing to increase grid resiliency: 1) implement 
targeted generation and DERs for reliability; 2) develop pockets of resiliency; and 3) build a 
lasting and stronger grid.  These objectives are aligned with the overarching REV objectives, 
such as “building a more resilient system” and “improving New York’s existing energy 
infrastructure,” as well as the clean energy goals in the State Energy Plan.

Advanced Planning & Asset Management 
Over the next 15 years National Grid plans to take a targeted approach to reliability and 
resiliency using Advanced Planning and Asset Management (APAM) tools and techniques 
such as the “One System – One Model” (described in “Greening the Grid”), to identify optimal 
locations that provide value to National Grid’s customers and account for many different 
variables such as: 
• Customer needs 
• Reliability 
• Grid congestion 
• Economic development 
• DER assets 
• Aging assets 
• Risk of extreme events 
By combining these various layers of information and forecasts, National Grid aims to 
prioritize spending in locations that provide the most benefits.  For example, an area with 
critical customers (e.g., hospitals, first responders, etc.) located adjacent to a river at high 
risk of flooding, could benefit from a project targeted at improving reliability and resiliency.  
Such a project could consist of asset replacements, substation storm hardening, installing 
insulated conductors, increasing voltage class to 15 kV, and integrating both DG and ESS to 
create a microgrid with increased reliability and resiliency. National Grid has already begun 
these types of analyses, specifically to identify and analyze distribution and sub-
transmission NWA opportunities related to reliability and resiliency.  
The transmission system will continue to meet North American Electric Reliability 
Corporation (NERC), Northeast Power Coordinating Council (NPCC), and the New York State 
Reliability Council (NYSRC) reliability standards.  As generation patterns change, new 
stresses and strains may occur.  Annual studies will continue to be conducted as dictated by 
NERC and the NYISO.  The Company will continue to run and analyze additional sensitivity 
cases to guide the evolution of the transmission system. 
Microgrids 
A microgrid is a self-sufficient smart grid that leverages many of the technologies previously 
mentioned, such as automatic load transfer and optimized voltage and power factor control.  
Microgrids can offer reliability and resiliency in the event of a major catastrophic event, such 
as hurricanes.  National Grid plans to continue exploring cost-effective ways to build and 
Advanced 
Planning & Asset 
Management
Microgrids
Smart Grid

Page 49 of 317 
 
integrate microgrids at appropriate locations in partnership with customers and third 
parties, each contributing the right skills and capabilities necessary. For example, National 
Grid plans to bring its expertise in system planning and design to help ensure each microgrid 
will perform as anticipated during a catastrophic event (e.g., integrating stronger overhead 
wires or undergrounding sections into the design to ensure resiliency). The Company is 
evaluating opportunities for ESS to improve resiliency by allowing the storage to island rural 
portions of the grid, with a concept coined “Rural Reliability.” In this concept, ESS is placed 
near the end of a radial sub transmission or transmission line with high exposure to 
reliability events (e.g., due to high tree or motor vehicle exposure) to act as a second source. 
Five locations are under preliminary investigation, and the Company is already exploring 
procurement for several of these location (through NWA and similar mechanisms outlined 
in the recent NY Storage Order).29 
Smart Grid 
National Grid is currently conducting a demonstration project using smart grid technologies 
in Clifton Park, New York.  The Company is also learning from the experiences of its 
Massachusetts affiliate, which has engaged in a Smart Energy Solutions pilot project in 
Worcester, Massachusetts.  Both projects include testing smart meters, AMI, and VVO 
technologies (see Chapter 7).   
Smart meter technology provides increased reliability and resiliency by delivering “last 
gasp” functionality that can send out a communication signal when grid supply is lost.  This 
information can be dispatched through an AMI system to alarm the control center with the 
location within a very short duration.  This information is used to determine the fault 
location and dispatch line crews even before customer phone calls are received.   
FLISR can also increase reliability and resiliency by reducing the impact of interruptions on 
the distribution system through the installation of automated switches along the main line 
and tie points of a feeder.  This allows a fault to be automatically isolated into a sub-section 
of the feeder. The remaining uninvolved feeder sub-sections can be resupplied by automated 
tie points, reducing both impacted customers and outage duration. National Grid has 
successfully completed 11 Distribution Automation schemes across Upstate NY and plans to 
deploy 10 FLISR schemes in Fiscal Year 2022.  
National Grid will continue its existing reliability and resiliency efforts, such as storm 
hardening, asset replacements, and system upgrades.  However, over time the Company 
expects its reliability and resiliency efforts will increasingly benefit from customer and third-
party owned assets such as DERs, with participation that may eventually be driven by DSP 
market-based products.

Investment Plan 
Subject to continuing regulatory support, National Grid plans to make foundational 
investments in cyber secure smart grid technologies (e.g., grid modernization and AMI), 
focusing on NWAs, and increasing investment in microgrids over time.  These investments 
look to offset or reduce traditional expenditures where possible.  National Grid intends to 
use data and analysis enabled by smart grid technologies to inform and prioritize equipment 
repair or replacement.  For example, transformer monitoring systems like Dissolved Gas 
Analysis (DGA) and substation condition monitoring may be utilized instead of regularly 
scheduled inspections.  This approach could help shift spending from traditional programs 
to smart grid projects, potentially reducing customer bill impacts.

NY Prize Microgrid Example  
National Grid is currently working on two NY Prize microgrid projects: 
• University Heights 
• Syracuse Community 
Each microgrid is unique due to location, customer types, and existing electrical 
infrastructure.  Therefore, National Grid is working with developers and customers to 
produce optimal designs for all stakeholders, based on the Company’s knowledge of the grid.  
Similarly, National Grid is proposing a hybrid ownership and operation model for all four 
microgrids, namely: 
• Third parties and/or customers own all DER assets; 
• Third parties can participate in electricity markets without violating any grid 
constraints; 
• National Grid is responsible for grid and island modes of operation as a regulated 
entity; and 
• National Grid owns all traditional microgrid wires-based distribution assets (existing 
& new).

National Grid’s approach in setting out its 15-year roadmap brings together the themes 
presented in the preceding chapters into an actionable path towards maximizing the value, 
safety, and service the grid can provide to customers. 
 
The four themes in the diagram above represent the Company’s key focus as the DSP. The 
amalgamation of the programs, projects, and policies described throughout this document 
will continue to evolve the grid to be greener, more resilient, and more economically and 
technically efficient. By the time 15 years has passed, the Company will be able to look back 
and point to the distinct steps it took in alignment with this Plan as progressing National Grid 
and NY as forward thinking leaders in the energy space. 
While the shared vision of a clean energy future for National Grid and NY State seems clear,  
the pathway is obstructed by risk and uncertainty.  Nonetheless, we must progress to a 
renewable and more resilient grid in a timely and cost-effective manner. This will not happen

Topic Catalog: 1. Advanced Metering Systems 
1.1 Introduction 
Advanced metering systems are comprised of state-of-the-art electronic/digital hardware and 
software, which combine interval data measurement with continuously available remote 
communications. These systems enable the measurement of detailed, time-based information 
(such as energy usage) and the frequent collection and transmittal of such information over a 
two-way communications network.  AMI typically refers to the full measurement and collection 
system which includes meters at the customer site, communication networks between the 
customer and a service provider, such as an electric, gas, or water utility, and data reception 
and management systems that make the information available to the service provider. 
The Commission is considering the Company’s proposal to implement AMI, changing the way 
customers interact with their energy and aligning the State’s critical policy objectives with 
operational requirements and customer benefits. AMI will provide customers with the 
knowledge and tools needed to better inform their energy decisions and manage their energy 
costs.  At the same time, AMI will modernize the Company’s system, enabling improved 
planning and operations, and the integration of increasing levels of DER to support a cleaner, 
more resilient and efficient system, consistent with the REV objectives and New York State’s 
clean energy goals as set forth in the CLCPA.  AMI will also provide the infrastructure and 
capabilities necessary to support the development and integration of distribution markets, in 
furtherance of the Company’s role as the DSP provider. 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16)

Assumptions: 
➢ The Company undertook an extensive stakeholder collaborative process, developing a 
refined business case, and completing a comprehensive Customer Engagement Plan, 
among other requirements pursuant to the Joint Proposal approved by Order of the 
Commission on March 15, 2018 in Case 17-E-0238; 
➢ The Company is awaiting Commission action on November 15, 2018 AMI update filing; 
➢ Upon receiving regulatory approval, the Company will sign contracts for external 
support, and commence a six-year deployment.  The deployment period will consist of 
two years of detailed design and back-office systems installation, followed by four years 
of electric meter, gas module, and network deployment; 
➢ Fiscal years 2020 and 2021 coincide with the final two years of the Company’s current 
rate plan.  If the six-year deployment commences during this timeframe, the Company 
will defer the associated revenue requirement of the AMI-related expenditures for 
recovery in the Company’s next rate case; and 
➢ To the extent the Company’s Rhode Island and Massachusetts affiliates receive approval 
to deploy AMI technology, the Company proposes to share the costs associated with the 
Service Company’s shared infrastructure, as well as ongoing operation and 
maintenance (O&M) costs among such affiliates.  AMI cost sharing among jurisdictions 
will drive further savings for customers.   
 
1.2 Drivers: 
 
The Company fully supports the Commission’s REV objectives and the State’s clean energy 
goals.  The AMI smart meter technology is foundational to National Grid’s ability to deliver 
on the new energy future embodied therein.   
  
With AMI, the Company will be better positioned to develop and deploy solutions aimed at 
achieving clean energy goals.  Among other benefits, AMI will support grid modernization 
and distributed system platform (DSP) planning functions, such as demand modeling, load 
forecasting, hosting capacity analysis, and capital investment planning, that will promote the 
development of a more dynamic, efficient, sustainable, and reliable energy network capable 
of serving future generations of utility customers.  AMI will also serve as a foundation for 
innovative rate design opportunities.  Moreover, AMI will provide customers with more 
information and greater control over their energy usage and associated costs, the 
opportunity to participate in future innovative pricing plans, and the ability to choose new 
solutions from third-party vendors participating in an animated energy market.

Without AMI, the Company will be challenged to implement all the necessary strategies 
needed to meet ambitious GHG reduction targets.  Additionally, the Company will lag behind 
other utilities in the country, with 90 million smart meter installations in the US projected 
by 2020 (i.e., 70% of the total market).  The Company’s customers expect, and the Company 
is committed to delivering, the same level of expanded service and benefits that AMI is 
capable of providing. 
 
The Company’s AMI proposal is driven by a commitment to advancing a clean energy future.  
It is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to align the State’s critical policy objectives with 
operational requirements and customer benefits, as the Company’s existing metering 
infrastructure is approaching life-cycle replacement.  In furtherance of achieving these 
shared clean energy goals, the Company requested the Commission approve its November 
2018 proposal to deploy AMI across National Grid’s service territory. 
 
As shown in the following table, in the absence of AMI, the Company anticipates replacing 
the majority of its metering assets (96 percent of electric meters and 80 percent of gas 
modules) by the end of fiscal year 2025.  The Company’s AMI deployment, which includes 
provisions to complete the installation of AMI technology by the end of fiscal year 2025, will 
serve to avoid the replacement costs of the legacy AMR electric meters and gas modules, 
while at the same time providing additional grid and customer benefits.

Drivers 
Alignment to the driver  
Efficient integration of 
DER  
By investing in AMI, the Company will be taking a key step 
toward achieving REV objectives and further developing the 
DSP.  In its role as DSP provider, the Company will construct, 
operate, and maintain highly integrated technology platforms, 
allowing the incorporation of third-party owned DERs, which 
can include DR, EE, energy storage, DG, and other on-site 
generation. These technologies will be integrated into the 
Company’s distribution infrastructure.  Ultimately, enhanced 
monitoring and control of these resources may support the 
establishment of a marketplace where services from these 
resources can be exchanged between Energy Service Companies 
(ESCOs), aggregators, customers, and other interested parties. 
Customer benefits 
Consumers are now accustomed to higher levels of service and 
convenience owing to the application of advanced technology 
and big data across industries.  Understanding how customers’ 
diverse and evolving needs manifest in their utility experience is 
the key to developing a higher value energy experience.  While 
reliability and affordability remain the foundation of the 
Company’s services, the Company must respond to an 
expanding customer demand for visibility, control, choice, and 
convenience in their energy experience.  AMI enables a higher 
value customer experience by providing granular, time-variant 
energy price signals, which enable a reduction in energy 
consumption and usage shift from high cost periods to lower 
cost periods, while also driving system savings.  Following are 
customer benefits envisioned through AMI implementation: 
 
Easier move in/out process  AMI provides the ability to connect 
and disconnect electric service remotely and in near real time, 
reducing the need for manual connects and disconnects31. This 
can improve the experience for customers when starting and 
stopping service. 
 
Customer Service Enhancements  Customer service 
representatives can use AMI data to enhance customer 
interactions. For example, AMI will: 
• Allow customer service representatives to send a signal 
to the meter to determine voltage levels or whether an 
outage is due to customer-owned equipment; 
                                                          
31 Any remote connections or disconnections will be done in accordance with applicable laws and 
regulations, including the Home Energy Fair Practices Act (“HEFPA”).

• Allow for real-time reconnects of electric meters; and 
• Provide historic information about prior outages and 
voltages. 
 
More 
actionable 
information 
and 
enhanced 
energy 
management  The deployment of AMI will enable customers to 
access their energy usage data in near real time, with granularity 
at sub-hourly reading intervals. As part of its proposal, National 
Grid will build and operate a Customer Energy Management 
Platform, to include an energy monitoring portal, which will act 
as a hub for residential, commercial and industrial customers to 
view their energy usage (i.e., AMI interval data). The Customer 
Energy Management Platform will also unlock new features and 
enhanced tools for customers to better connect them to 
personalized programs and services, such as the Company’s 
existing E-Commerce Platform, Solar Marketplace, and Dynamic 
Load Management programs. 
 
New and innovative pricing options  AMI deployment, coupled 
with an enhanced customer platform, will enable the Company 
to offer innovative mass-market time varying rates (TVR). This 
will provide customers with pricing signals to manage energy 
costs, through actions such as reducing energy consumption or 
shifting energy use to lower-cost periods. This has the additional 
benefit of reducing overall system demand and energy costs by 
displacing peak period consumption for activities such as EV 
charging. Enhancing customer knowledge and control over 
energy use and the total energy bill is at the heart of REV and 
next-generation customer engagement. AMI will provide the 
ability to deliver flexible rate options that are unattainable with 
the Company’s current AMR meters. 
 
Access to third-party services  Solutions, tools, and services 
enabled by AMI must also prioritize third-party connectivity. By 
animating the market for new industry participants, third-
parties will be able to bring additional value to customers 
through products and services such as home/building energy 
management and smart EV charging. Collaboration between the 
Company and external partners can enable a robust and 
personalized customer experience. Customers and third-party 
vendors will likewise have increased access to more granular 
energy data through Green Button Connect My Data and home-
area network functionality. National Grid has deployed Green 
Button Download My Data for current customers and plans to 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16)

provide customer-authorized Green Button Connect My Data 
functionality in advance of AMI deployment. 
 
Enhanced customer alerting and personalization tools  
Customer access to timely, granular energy consumption 
information is an important driver and enabler of behavioral 
changes. Enhanced data can reduce energy consumption, 
increase energy affordability, and reduce bill volatility through 
services such as high-bill alerts. In addition, the Company’s 
customer service representatives can leverage this data to 
proactively identify relevant programs and offers for customers, 
enabling more accurate, personalized and actionable responses 
to customer needs. The Company anticipates that this, in turn, 
will drive greater program participation and improved program 
outcomes. 
 
Enablement of smart-home devices  AMI will allow customers 
to better manage their energy consumption through the use of 
smart devices such as thermostats, water heaters and other 
appliances that can be integrated with AMI.  Capabilities enabled 
through a home-area network, inclusive of home energy 
management systems, will be configurable to send and receive 
secure communications to and from the Company or third-party 
market entities. With a customer’s authorization, the system can 
automatically adjust energy consumption in response to pricing 
signals and curtailment events. The Company currently executes 
similar functionality through its Dynamic Load Management 
programs but envisions more advanced capabilities following 
the deployment of AMI. 
 
Outage Management 
AMI has the ability to report a customer outage in near real time, 
without the need to rely on notification from a customer or 
substation monitoring. The functionality also allows the 
Company to send a signal to AMI meters to identify areas that 
still require restoration and confirm when all outages have been 
restored. This functionality will improve situational awareness 
contributing to reduced restoration costs and improved outage 
response.

Manage bill impacts 
to customers and keep 
costs in check 
In addition to the robust customer engagement activities 
included in the recently filed Customer Engagement Plan, the 
Company also proposed a one-year period for customers to 
learn about their meters before the new rate structure takes 
effect, followed by a bill guarantee for all customers in the first 
year they are on TVR (i.e., the second year after meter 
installation).  The guarantee will be based on a comparison of 
the customer’s annual charges under the TVR model and what 
the customer will have otherwise paid under the Company’s 
standard volumetric rate for that same twelve month period.  If 
the customer paid more under the TVR structure, the customer 
will be credited that amount to ensure he or she paid no more 
than the basic volumetric rate in the first year.  In addition, if a 
“new” customer (one who has not been at a premise served by 
the Company since the introduction of TVR) moves into the 
service territory, the customer will also receive the one-year bill 
guarantee. 
 
For income-eligible customers, the Company plans to continue 
to offer an extended bill guarantee period on a graduated basis. 
In year three after installation of the smart meter, the Company 
will compare the income-eligible customer’s annual charges 
under the TVR model and what the customer will have 
otherwise paid under the Company’s standard volumetric rate 
for the same twelve month period.  If the comparison shows the 
low-income customer paid more than five percent above what 
he or she will have otherwise paid under the Company’s current 
basic volumetric supply rate for the entire twelve months, the 
customer will be credited that amount above 5 percent.  The 
guarantee will extend to year four after meter installation with 
a limit of ten percent above what the customer will have 
otherwise paid under the Company’s basic volumetric supply 
rate for the entire twelve month period.  As with non-income-
eligible customers, if a “new” income-eligible customer (one 
who has not been at a premise served by the Company since the 
introduction of TVR) moves into the service territory, the 
income-eligible customer will receive the one-year full bill 
guarantee, followed by the two-year partial bill guarantee.

System efficiency 
goals  
Through educational initiatives and pricing signals designed to 
encourage efficient consumption behavior, over time customers 
will proactively shift portions of their energy consumption to 
times of day where energy rates are lower, thereby resulting in 
reductions in their electric bills.  Shifting energy usage will also 
flatten the overall load curve.  This shift, combined with other 
offerings, such as VVO and EE, will lower energy peaks resulting 
in 
reduced 
delivery 
system 
and 
generation 
capacity 
expenditures. 
Encourage smart 
infrastructure 
investments that lead 
to growth, reliability, 
resiliency and 
enhanced power 
quality 
AMI granular, real-time load and voltage measurements support  
a number of grid modernization initiatives including HCA,  
Advanced Distribution Management System (ADMS), FLISR, and 
VVO that will enhance  reliability, resiliency and power quality.   
Cyber security and 
privacy 
The Company understands that in an evolving technology 
landscape, there are growing cyber security risks.  To best 
secure AMI, a comprehensive cyber security plan will 
incorporate proper end-to-end security controls into all aspects 
of design, implementation, and deployment of AMI meter 
technology.  These controls will secure and monitor all AMI 
meter devices, the communications infrastructure, and back-
office systems supporting them, along with user portals and 
other critical systems and components. 
 
The Company will leverage industry-leading best practices to 
meet the goals of a robust cyber security program, such as 
defining the Company’s encryption practices to ensure the 
encryption of any data transmitted across the network follows 
recognized standards and protocols. Other practices include 
robust training, change control, configuration management 
security, access monitoring, incident management, end-to-end 
encryption, network segmentation, and firewalls. These cyber 
security measures will enable the Company to maintain 
confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the systems and its 
information in both the short and long-term with AMI.
