The Company is committed to protecting customer data and has 
developed a thorough Data Privacy Plan. The Plan involves a 
three-tiered approach with: 1) a commitment to core data 
privacy policies; 2) regular assessments of the Company’s 
performance; and 3) constant vigilance to protect customer 
data.  National Grid has implemented reasonable physical, 
technical, and administrative security measures to safeguard 
smart meter energy usage data.  
 
National Grid only collects smart meter energy usage data that 
are reasonably required to provide utility services to customers, 
approved by regulatory agencies, and authorized by law.  The 
Company does not collect any personally identifiable 
information (PII) through customers’ smart meters.  Of the 
approved information, the Company will only collect, process, 
retain, use, and disclose smart meter energy usage data for 
legitimate National Grid utility related business purposes, or as 
specified by a customer’s express consent to disclose such 
information to a third party (e.g., Green Button Connect My Data 
or the electronic data interchange (EDI) used to send 
information to energy service companies (ESCOs)). 
 
Customers must provide consent prior to the Company sharing 
their meter data with third parties.  Customers are given the 
opportunity to choose whether to share their smart meter data 
with third parties through the Green Button Connect My Data 
program, arrangements with an ESCO, or some other secure 
technical or programmatic method that complies with 
applicable rules and regulations.  Similarly, the Company retains 
smart meter data for the period reasonably necessary to carry 
out its business functions and services, unless a longer retention 
period is required by law.

Horizon 2 (6-15 years):   
AMI deployment will allow the Company to provide more granular, time-variant price

1.5 Challenges: 
 
Process Design:  
Process design is an extremely important component upon which program development and 
organizational change depend.  As many of the Company’s employees will be impacted by 
the deployment of AMI (including meter-field technicians, meter-shop technicians, customer 
service representatives, control center operators, billing analysts, and others), the Company 
has started assessing each area to understand the total business impact of the change 
brought by AMI. From there, the Company will develop a plan to aid in the smooth transition 
for both customers and employees including defining how the technology will be used.  
 
Change Management:  
Change management is an important factor in the successful implementation of AMI. The 
Company’s change management effort will encompass all tools, processes, and activities 
required to successfully deliver change within the Company, deliver the associated benefits, 
and support the specific business objectives related to AMI. This methodology is based on 
the belief that reactions and behaviors at different stages of a change process can be 
predicted, measured, and managed. Doing so allows the Company to assess how the change 
initiative is progressing and adjust course based on that assessment to ensure a successful 
outcome.  
 
Customer Engagement:  
Customer Engagement is critical to realizing the benefits enabled by AMI. The Company 
recognizes that customers will require education, training, and knowledge of the tools 
provided in order to become active participants in managing their energy and realizing the 
benefits enabled by AMI. For example, customers will need to be engaged and knowledgeable 
about any new pricing options available through AMI, such as Time Varying Rates (TVR), in 
order to understand how to adjust their energy usage to lower their monthly bill. The 
Company is committed to ensuring that all customers have the information needed to help 
them leverage AMI to manage their energy costs and has developed a comprehensive 
Customer Engagement Plan (CEP) in order to do so.

Topic Catalog: 2. Asset Maturity (AMS/BMS) 
2.1 Introduction 
The Company is on a journey to improve its Asset Management activities. Asset Management is 
much more than just the physical maintenance of assets, it is the holistic approach to realizing 
value from all asset types, including all activities involved in the asset’s life cycle.  Providing 
sustainable outcomes for the Company’s customers requires operations and maintenance cost 
savings, asset life extension, and business risk reduction. This requires a common approach to 
asset management, that focuses on addressing the most important issues and opportunities while 
making sure assets contribute to the organizational objectives.

strengthen the business, the Company can  be more resilient and deliver the goals of the 
business.

2.3 Implementation Plan: 
 
The Company approved a new Business Management Standard (BMS) for Asset Management 
and engineering in 2019 that lays out the minimum requirements for our Asset Systems, 
lifecycle delivery options and continued improvement. The Asset Systems include planning, 
development, design, installation, and program management of energy networks, energy 
plants, and other energy installations. Life cycle delivery is the maintenance, repair, 
replacement, operation and retirement of assets. 
To meet the BMS for Asset Management and become “best in class” for asset management, 
the Company is working to utilize practices based on the ISO 55001 Asset Management, the 
Institute of Asset Management’s “Asset Management – An Anatomy”, and “The Asset 
Management Landscape” published by the Global Forum on Maintenance and Asset 
Management (GFMAM).  To help with understanding the Company’s current state of asset 
management and develop its capabilities an external consultant (AMCL) conducted a review 
of the Company’s policies, procedures and work practices as part of an Asset Management 
Maturity Assessment gap analysis. The finding of this assessment was used to create an asset 
management improvement roadmap for each business unit. The focus of these 
improvements is outlined below.  
Asset Management Strategy and Planning: 
The Company is developing a clear line of sight between the corporate objectives and the 
asset management activities. This allows employees to understand how their work 
contributes to Company goals. This includes a clear Asset Management policy that is 
composed of the principles and requirements used to determine the Company’s Asset 
Management Objectives and long-term approach for the management of its distribution and 
transmission electric assets.  
The Company is updating its guidance on decision-making to enable a consistent approach. 
This includes updated criteria for evaluating risk, costs, performance, and condition. Having 
standard criteria allows comparability and consistency across the business in making capital 
and expense decisions that are in line with the Asset Management Objectives.   
Asset Management Decision Making: 
The Company is incorporating a criticality-based prioritization with its condition-based 
replacement decisions, so customers realize the maximum value from assets. Investments to 
maintain or replace assets focuses on areas that will yield the greatest benefits.  
The Company is developing a series of Key Strategies to provide a consistent approach to 
project development. The initial strategies include a US Electric Maintenance Strategy, 
supporting Asset Class Strategies, and an Outage Management Strategy.

The Maintenance strategy sets forth the approach for the US Electric business to determine 
the maintenance requirements for different asset types based on the criticality and levels of 
deterioration.    To support this, the Company is developing a maintenance analysis process 
that utilizes Failure Mode Effects Analyses (FMEA) to standardize the process to develop 
risk-based maintenance regimes that prioritize maintenance activities to prevent failures 
that are difficult to detect and have a great impact on the reliability of the asset. 
Asset Class Strategies are being developed for applicable asset classes. These strategies 
identify the optimum lifecycle delivery options for all stages of the asset’s life. This includes 
historical information based on past performance, asset inventory, and financial justification 
for all lifecycle delivery option including capital, maintenance, and disposal strategies. The 
standardized use of whole life costing in maintenance and replacement decisions identifies 
what the expected lowest cost option is to maximize the life of the asset while balancing the 
associated environmental, safety, reliability, and financial risks due to an asset’s unreliability 
or failure.  
Due to the increasing costs of maintaining a high level of reliably the Outage Management 
Strategy evaluates the cost and risk tradeoff associated with taking planned outages. This 
includes evaluating using fewer and potentially longer outages verses taking additional 
shorter outages to complete maintenance or replacements. This strategy also evaluates the 
impact of combing work that may be due at different times to minimize the total cost of 
taking outages.  
The use of consistent ranking criteria for asset health and replacement priority’s based on 
documented data will enable a consistent approach to determine the optimum maintain and 
replace intervals.  Combing the Asset Health criteria with the assets criticality or importance 
factor will allow a more optimized and targeted approach to maintenance and capital 
projects that focuses the work on assets that provide the greatest benefit and result in an 
acceptable level of risk.  
To ensure this standard decision making is used for all projects, the capital planning process 
will be refined so that projects are identified consistently and align with the organizational 
objects.  This will be done through documenting how each investment contributes to meeting 
the US Electrics Asset Management Objectives. This will also include enhanced business case 
guidance so that the documentation prepared for each project contains the appropriate 
details of the project’s asset management value, risk profile, costs (including avoided costs) 
and impacts. This allows appropriate evaluation at the time a project is presented for 
inclusion into the capital plan. 
Lifecycle Delivery: 
Lifecycle delivery ensures that the proper financial and operations decisions are made 
throughout the life of the asset.  The cycle begins at acquisition, through operation and 
maintenance and ends when the asset is disposed.  By properly utilizing and monitoring the 
Company’s assets, the correct decisions can be made throughout the life cycle, thus 
benefiting the customer.

Integrated Transmission Asset Management (iTAM) is a critical part of asset management 
decision making and upgrading information technology (IT) systems to enhance asset 
management capabilities.  The iTAM program will stand up platforms for Enterprise Asset 
Management (EAM), Asset Performance Management (APM), and Asset Investment Planning 
(AIP) while also integrating with and/or upgrading existing platforms used for Capital 
Project Management (CPM), Geographic Information Systems (GIS), and Financial & Plant 
Accounting (F&PA). 
Information Systems, Data, Tools, and Integrations used to advance National Grid asset 
management objectives are under-utilized, antiquated, and/or non-existent.  As-is 
technology architecture, inventory, and transmission system roadmaps are limited.    
National Grid kicked-off the planning phase of iTAM to drive collaboration with IT, 
Transmission business personnel and support staff to review, assess, explicitly articulate, 
and plan technology requirements to empower operational capabilities so that the US 
electric business successfully adapts to a changing industry landscape as well as customer 
expectations.  
A major component of the iTAM roadmap involves the implementation of industry leading 
IT systems to address key shortcomings:  
• 
Absence of a unified Asset Management tool gives rise to a dependency on 
external department resources, complicating timely task completion and hindering 
facilitation of stakeholder and internal informational requests.  
• 
Disparate systems which are in silo or only partially integrated (requiring 
significant manual interventions to bridge connectivity and/or functionality gaps), 
inhibits comprehensive network knowledge and risk assessment, stifling investment 
prioritizations and decisions.  
• 
Data stored in multiple systems creating duplicative and sometimes 
conflicting records leading to data accuracy concerns and inefficiencies.  In many 
cases, data is difficult to access, compile, validate, or analyze as needed to unleash 
actionable results.

Topic Catalog: 3. Dynamic Load Management 
3.1 Introduction 
Dynamic Load Management (DLM) programs actively target reductions to peak demand during hours 
of high expected demand and/or reliability problems. The DLM programs enable utilities and operating 
areas, such as the New York Independent System Operator (NYISO), to take action in response to a system 
reliability concerns or economic (pricing) signals. During these events customers can actively participate 
by either cutting their load or by turning on a generator to displace load from behind the customer’s meter. 
The Company currently operates DLM programs that have been approved by the Commission. The 
Company’s DLM programs consist of: the Distribution Load Relief Program (DLRP); the 
Commercial System Relief Program (CSRP); and the Direct Load Control (DLC) program. The DLRP 
and CSRP are focused on commercial & industrial customers, whereas the DLC program is a 
residential and small-commercial customer-focused program.

DLM Programs provide a mechanism for customers to control their energy usage with 
potential opportunities to receive financial incentives for their actions.  These DLM Programs 
encourage customer engagement and participation in energy management, while directly 
reducing electrical load when it is economic to do so. In return, overall system reliability and 
efficiency is improved for all customers.

3.3 Implementation Plan:   
The Company’s DLM programs consist of: 
Distribution Load Relief Program: 
 
The DLRP is a contingency program activated 
for system critical situations. These include 
unforeseen distribution system emergencies 
where stressed electrical equipment may 
exceed limits. Events for the DLRP are called 
with short or no advance notice, which are 
considered “immediate” events, or they are 
called at least two hours in advance, in which 
case 
they 
are 
considered 
“test” 
or 
“contingency” events.  Calling the DLRP to 
address a contingency event can reduce the 
potential for a system overload, thereby 
providing reliability benefits and can also 
reduce the need for and resultant costs of a 
traditional utility investment. This program 
currently has no customers enrolled in the 
program.  
 
While this program still currently exists within 
the DLM Portfolio, the incentive levels for this 
program have been set to zero to preserve the 
restarting of the program in the future. There 
are no customers enrolled in the program.  
 
Commercial System Relief Program:  
The CSRP is activated for peak shaving needs. 
For “Planned Events”, the Company provides 
notice at least 21 hours in advance.  The 
“Planned Event” may last four hours or more. 
For “Unplanned Events” the Company will 
provide notice less than 21 hours in advance.  
Calling the CSRP to address a contingency can 
reduce the potential for a system overload, 
thereby providing reliability benefits.  The 
CSRP can also reduce the need for and 
resultant 
costs 
of 
a 
traditional 
utility

time sign up payment and yearly incentive that is payable the second year of participation 
for reducing load during 80 percent of called events/hours.

emergencies and manage VTOU rates. As the number of aggregators increases, the

expansion will also focus on technological advances, changes in incentive rate structures 
and sustainable markets.

Topic Catalog: 4. Dissolved Gas Analysis 
4.1 Introduction 
The breakdown of electrical insulating materials and related components inside a transformer 
generates gases within the transformer.  The identity of the gases being generated can be very useful 
information in a preventive maintenance program.  Dissolved Gas Analysis (DGA) is an internal 
measurement from the network transformer fluid or head gas space that is used to evaluate the 
overall health of the network transformer.  
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 573 of 1030


--- Page 93 ---
Page 92 of 317 
 
Assumptions: 
➢ Using DGA to evaluate network transformers will provide data for asset condition 
benchmarking; 
➢ Costs for manual sampling will decrease as more DGA monitors are installed; and 
➢ DGA data will allow the Company to replace transformers before they fail. 
 
4.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customer - Customers will benefit from DGA monitoring systems that will allow 
the Company to evaluate the health of transformer fluid.  With this valuable asset condition 
information, the Company can remove and replace network transformers before they fail, 
also avoiding customer outages.

The Company will install the DGA monitoring system in several stages, beginning with a 
benchmarking pilot in the fall of 2017.  Based on the results of the pilot, the current target 
anticipates installing the technology on approximately 20 percent of the system over 15 
years.   
The Company has approximately 875 network transformers in the Upstate New York 
service territory.  The 15-year plan will target 175 network transformers to be equipped 
with the DGA monitoring system.

Topic Catalog: 5. Distributed Generation 
5.1 Introduction 
Distributed Generation (DG) systems generally consist of customer-sponsored, small-scale 
generators connected in parallel with the utility.  DG systems are smaller in MW rating than 
centralized power generation, and they are usually tied to the distribution system of the grid 
rather than the transmission system.  DG systems are becoming more popular due to incentives 
for clean energy, the REV proceeding, and social benefit goals.  The Company is actively engaged 
in advancing these important initiatives to encourage the growth of DG, while ensuring the safety, 
reliability, and power quality of the electric system.   
Exhibit__(EIOP-16)

be carbon-free electricity by 2040, will drive increased customer DER installations.  The

➢ A preliminary technical screening analysis for complex DG projects. 
5.4 Road Map: 
 
Horizon 1 (1-5 years):  
The Company has many programs and pilots listed above to look for ways to continuously 
improve the customer experience for connecting DER to the electric system in the next 5 
years.  Adjustments are being made to better accommodate projects with multiple 
generation sources, most commonly solar projects paired with energy storage systems.  
The Company will continue to make improvements to the IOAP, including more customer 
interaction and the ability to automate preliminary screens.   
Hosting capacity maps will be maturing in the next couple of years and should give more 
specific direction to customers on ideal places on the feeder to interconnect DER to manage 
upgrade costs.  The Company will evaluate DER options for NWA to address capacity 
concerns.  The Company will commence large-scale installation of smart meters that will 
help obtain better data for engineering decisions, improve operation of the distribution 
system, and may potentially be used for more monitoring and control of DER systems. 
Energy storage applications will increase in volume in response to the Energy Storage 
Order.  This technology still has relatively low volumes of penetration and existing systems 
will be evaluated for best practices to integrate into the grid, allowing for integrating 
increasing amounts of DG into the electric distribution system, as well as providing capacity 
and other needed services in targeted parts of the distribution system.  Paired DG and ESS 
are an example of technology combinations that will provide value to the grid. 
New York’s New Green Deal has more aggressive renewable energy goals.  With incentives 
and market signals to support these goals, the volume of applications for solar PV, energy 
storage systems, and other types of DG will be scaled up in coming years.

DER saturation could be a risk at this horizon.  Developers may be more dependent on

as the 2p.u. voltage threshold (i.e., the maximum transient over voltage limit for the EPS) in 
a transmission ground fault overvoltage condition.

start to become a concern in this timeframe.  As systems wear down, the Company will need 
to prepare for contingencies if a developer decides to retire a generator rather than 
maintain or replace the units.   
5.5 Challenges: 
 
National Grid’s service territory is a challenge in that roughly half of the distribution system is 5 
kV, with limited capacity for DG growth.  The lower voltage 5 kV systems typically have less load 
than 15 kV circuits, and they have more restrictions on distribution protection.  The Company 
does targeted conversions to bring circuits from 5 kV to 15 kV, but these are costly and the pace 
may not keep up with the demand for hosting capacity. 
Surges in DER applications have led to forecasting challenges, and the uneven surges of 
applications are expected to continue.  Surges can be caused by changes in the SIR, when 
developers perceive one version as more favorable than another, such as the potential for 
increasing the DG project net-metering eligibility cap from 2 MW to 5 MW, or market incentives, 
tax incentives, or conditions that may cap, grandfather or shift financial viability of a given 
project.  New developers sometimes submit large numbers of applications at one time to 
determine which applications will best fit their business model.  These irregular flows add 
challenges to forecasting an appropriate budget and resource plan to ensure the utility can flex to 
meet peaks and valleys in the DER workload while balancing all of the other work in the overall 
portfolio.   The queue management process introduced into the SIR in 2017 has helped mitigate 
DER application surge impacts, although risks of future surges exist. 
Renewable DER is an important element of the REV clean energy goals.  Policies are frequently 
adjusting to respond to customer and utility needs, to encourage more DER installation. National 
Grid has an active voice at forums such as the IPWG (Interconnection Policy Working Group) and 
ITWG (Interconnection Technical Working Group) to drive policy and standards to support 
finding new ways to increase DER integration capacity and leveraging these new technologies to 
better plan and operate the electric system.  These groups are comprised of a number of relevant 
stakeholders, including utility technical representatives, solar and energy storage developers, 
and others from the DG community, who meet regularly to explore possible technical and policy

Topic Catalog: 6. Economic Development 
6.1 Introduction 
The Company’s economic development efforts are designed to promote regional economic 
growth – new jobs and capital investment – through the attraction, expansion, and retention of 
businesses in communities throughout National Grid’s service territory.   These activities include 
incentive programs (grants and delivery discount programs) as well as “core” economic 
development services – helping customers locate sites and buildings that best meet their needs 
in terms of utility infrastructure availability/capacity and other location factors, both energy and 
non-energy related.

 6.5 Challenges: 
 
A fundamental challenge in utility economic development is that the best sites in terms of 
available electric infrastructure and capacity are not necessarily (or even very often) the 
most desirable from an overall economic development perspective.  Criteria such as the 
amount of available acreage, site topography, workforce quality/availability, supply 
chain/transportation access, company culture and aesthetics (e.g., preferring an urban 
versus a rural or campus setting), availability of state/local incentives, and political 
considerations can all influence a customer to choose a location where a costly and time-
consuming infrastructure upgrade is required.  Attempts to redirect customers to sites with 
more robust infrastructure are often unrealistic or ineffective, as are attempts to dissuade 
the developer from continuing to market the site if it has many other assets.  In addition,

Topic Catalog:7. Electric Transportation 
7.1 Introduction 
The transportation sector is one of the largest contributors to anthropogenic U.S. greenhouse 
gas (GHG) emissions. Transportation accounted for the largest portion (29%) of total U.S. GHG 
emissions in 2017 and for 34% of New York’s GHG emissions. These emissions continue to 
grow. This section summarizes how National Grid will help the State of New York achieve the 
ambitious CLCPA greenhouse gas (“GHG”) reduction levels and the State’s Zero Emissions 
Vehicle (ZEV) goals by catalyzing electric vehicle (EV) adoption. Timely action is necessary to 
meet these aggressive goals.  
The Company expects that Staff’s anticipated EV Whitepaper will provide guidance that 
significantly influences the EV initiatives the Company will undertake in the next five years.  
Nevertheless, the Company is not waiting on such guidance to act, and is implementing a suite 
of actions to promote increased and appropriate EV adoption in its service territory.  This 
section reviews the motivating drivers of the Transportation Plan and the specific actions that 
the Company has taken and will continue to take to encourage the EV market, including 
development of charging infrastructure, load management techniques and market education. 
This section also highlights areas of uncertainty where policy action and an increasingly 
sophisticated insight into electric usage around EVs will play a role.  
While the number of EVs in the Company’s service territory is currently small (8,300 as of 
December 2018), the Company anticipates meaningful growth over the term of this Plan. To 
date, the Company has developed and used a scenario-based top-down forecast for EVs in its 
service territory, but in planning for the future it has constructed a bottom-up forecast based 
on a more detailed modeling approach.

7.3 Implementation Plan:  
The Company has developed estimates for different scenarios covering a mix of different 
levels of future adoption of EVs. These scenarios include Percent of New Registrations based 
on historical adoption rates and the ZEV Memorandum of Understanding target.   
➢ Percent of New Registrations (PNR): This scenario uses the historical adoption rate 
from registration data. This scenario is determined as a function of new EV 
registrations each year as a percent of all new vehicle registrations.32  
➢ ZEV Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) target: This scenario assumes that EV 
adoption meets the ZEV target of about 840,00033 in New York by the year 2025. 
National Grid is assumed to account for a share of that goal as a function of its current 
share of EVs in its service territory as a percent of total EVs in the state (~190,000). 
Current levels of EVs are ramped up between now and the year 2025 to achieve those 
targets.

Residential EV Load Management:  
The Company offers a VTOU rate for residential customers to encourage off-peak electric 
usage as opposed to peak intervals.   Between the hours of 11pm and 7am, customers can 
obtain lower commodity and delivery rates.  The rate also includes a super-peak commodity 
price to discourage charging during summer peak periods.  EV drivers who receive supply 
service from National Grid have the option of receiving a one-time comparison of one year 
of charges on the VTOU versus the SC-1 standard tariff. If this comparison indicates they 
would have paid less on the SC-1 standard tariff rate, the Company will provide a one-time 
bill credit for the difference. More information about the VTOU rate is available here:  
https://www9.nationalgridus.com/niagaramohawk/home/rates/4_vtou.asp 
The VTOU rate for residential customers currently has low enrollment. The Company is 
exploring other options to incentivize managed charging and to appropriately value and 
reward the flexibility of EV charging.   
Commercial EV Load Management:  
Customers with EV charging stations take service under the applicable rates. Customers with 
less than 100 kW of demand will take service under SC-2. Inside of SC-2, customers with less 
than 2,000 kWh of usage per month would be on SC-ND (non-demand) while those with 
usage over 2,000 kWh will be on a demand-based delivery rate. Larger customers take 
service under SC-3. The Public Service Commission’s Standby Order allows all customers to 
opt into Standby Rates with both contract demand and daily-as-used demand charges for 
delivery and hour pricing along with a proper installed capacity (ICAP) tag for supply. The 
Commission has called the Standby rate the most “theoretically pure” rate design which 
sends the economically efficient signals for demand management.  
In order to lessen the impacts of demand charges in the preliminary phases of EV market 
growth, the Company offers an incentive to new, publicly accessible DC Fast Charging (DCFC) 
stations greater than 50 kW. The incentive declines over time and is payable annually. Up to 
300 plugs will be eligible to earn the incentive in National Grid’s upstate New York Service 
territory. Eligible plugs earn an incentive for every year which they are eligible between 
2019 and 2025. More information about the DCFC incentive is available here: 
https://www.nationalgridus.com/upstate-ny-business/energy-saving-programs/electric-
vehicle-charging-station-program.aspx

New Service Connection:  
The Company establishes new service for EVSE being installed by commercial customers.

individual charger power levels of 50 kW to 150 kW and above, and aggregated site power

developments to inform its load forecasts.  
EV Market Development:  
The Company operates a network of 66 public “Level 2” charging stations in its service 
territory, installed in partnership with a charging station service provider between 2011-
2014, using NYSERDA grant funds. Stations are owned and maintained by National Grid but 
operated by customers (site hosts) on their own meters. Locations are visible on 
Plugshare.com, and nearly 2,000 unique drivers from 1,000 different zip codes have used 
these stations since installation.   
The Company is in year two of National Grid’s three-year electric rate case, which includes a 
Phase 1 Electric Transportation Program with: (i) an EV charging host incentive program; 
and (ii) a consumer EV education program.  
i) The EV charging host incentive program is a “make ready” infrastructure program for 
electric vehicle charging stations.  This EVSE program enables commercial and industrial 
customers to install electric vehicle charging stations on their property with the intention of 
providing EV charging for tenants, customers and employees.  
 ii) The program also engages employees, tenants and customers by providing EV education 
program materials to each site host’s point of contact.  In addition, the site host is required 
to hold ride and drive events and provide periodic webinars to its distribution list.  The 
employees/tenants are provided access to National Grid’s “Drive Green with National Grid” 
website: https://drivegreen.nationalgridus.com/learn/.   
Through this program, the Company is also sending electric vehicle messaging to targeted 
customers across National Grid’s Upstate New York territory.  These customers are directed 
to the Drive Green website and associated car dealership leads, and sales are tracked. 
The program has already exceeded goals and projections.  The program is working with over 
150 customers yielding over 100 projects.  Stakeholders, described below, have also engaged 
customers and helped deliver more than half of the Company’s projects.

and actions to support EV market development. The Company continues to implement the

7.4 Road Map: 
 
Horizon 1 (1-5 years):  
The Company expects that Staff’s anticipated EV Whitepaper will provide guidance that 
significantly influences the EV initiatives the Company will undertake in the next five years.  
Nevertheless, the Company is not waiting on such guidance to act, and is implementing a 
suite of actions to promote increased and appropriate EV adoption in its service territory.  
EV load forecasts are currently incorporated into the Company’s total electric load forecast 
both at the system level and feeder level. To further improve EV forecasting, the Company 
is working to implement a transportation modeling approach to simulate the charging 
behaviors for both residential and non-residential EV chargers. Specifically, the 
transportation modeling approach will be developed based on a large-scale, open-source 
agent-based traffic simulation tool – POLARIS (Planning and Operations Language for 
Agent-based Regional Integrated Simulation)- developed by the Department of Energy.  
The transportation modeling approach will feature an integrated network-demand model 
such that all aspects of EV driving and charging decisions are modeled simultaneously.  
Survey data such as the National Household Travel Survey enables simulations which 
include departure time, destination choice, route choice, charging duration and location 
choice.  By considering EV and EV charger technologies, demographics, travel and charging 
preferences, and market adoption conditions, the transportation modeling results will 
complement the existing EV forecast by offering increased granularity into feeder level 
forecasts. Specifically, real-world EV charging data will be utilized to predict travelers’ 
charging preference (start time, duration, and start State-of-Charge) and battery charging 
properties (charging speed and energy use) for more realistic feeder-level load forecasts. 
Furthermore, the transportation modeling will seek to identify specific locations likely to

The Company’s vehicle adoption forecast scenarios diverge significantly by 2025, with the 
possibility of annual EV sales substantially higher than those seen today. However, the 
Company’s expectation is that 2025 system-wide load growth due to EVs, even in higher 
adoption cases, remains moderate and the existing system has flexibility to supply this load 
with relatively few modifications. The cost impact to supply this incremental load is assumed 
to be low, however localized impacts are likely to occur in areas which see clustered DCFC 
installations, geographic concentrations of L2 chargers, or areas that are already near system 
constraints.  
By 2030, likely EV load growth becomes significant enough to require meaningful additions 
to the Company’s capital plan.  For example, in the Buffalo area, the supply and distribution 
system are highly utilized and have limited capacity to supply new load depending on EV 
penetration.  Larger loads of 1 MW could be an issue with majority of the feeders in Buffalo.  
To supply the 2030 projected load, new investments would be required, including 
potentially two new or expanded substations.  In the Syracuse area, the electric system is 
also highly utilized and projected load could also potentially require a new or expanded 
substation.  In addition, if fast charging stations surpass the current expectations, 
infrastructure enhancements of the Company’s sub-transmission and transmission system 
along Interstates 81, 86, 87, 88 and 90 would be necessary.  The Company may explore 
partnerships with existing travel plaza operators to supply fast charging in sufficient 
volumes to support the longer-distance traveling public.  Additional substations may be 
required in this scenario.   The Company’s transmission network is generally parallel to the 
existing major passenger and freight rail routes in upstate NY.   Should the state pursue the 
electrification of the rail network, the Company is poised to support the effort with similar 
system enhancements for supplying EVs. 
Comprehensive area studies will be required to identify all the concerns and develop feasible 
options. However, the Company’s focus on development of managed charging and DR 
programs will better enable the EV load growth projected in 2030 and beyond while 
minimizing the required additions to the Company’s capital plan.

7.5 Challenges: 
 
Challenges for system integration and policy:  
High level of uncertainty in EV Adoption Rates:  
EV adoption scenarios show a wide range of possible adoption levels by customers. 
Additionally, while system wide impacts of EVs are expected to be low, localized system 
impacts due to clustered DCFC installations or geographically concentrated L2 chargers may 
be significant.  This high level of uncertainty makes it difficult for the Company to fully 
anticipate the significance of EVs as a factor in its system planning and operation.  To plan 
for such challenges, the Company is exploring off-peak charging, managed charging, and 
demand response initiatives so that they can mitigate future load increases.  Additionally, 
the Company has invested in the development of an EV & heat pump scenario generation 
tool to analyze how variations in study parameters influence the resulting penetration 
forecasts and subsequently, impacts to the grid. 
Lack of visibility into customer vehicle ownership:  
The Company has very limited visibility into specific customer EV ownership aside from 
customers who have reported an EV when registering for the VTOU rate. This prevents the 
company from targeting those owners specifically for EV programs. However, the Company 
does collect zip-code level data on vehicle registrations in National Grid territory through 
POLK, an automotive data company. This is used to help forecast the number of future EVs 
in the Company’s territory.  
Lack of data on charging impacts:  
The Company has limited information on the actual impact of EV charging on its electric 
system today (except for the simulation platform noted previously).  Without AMI, the 
Company cannot detect an EV being charged by a residential customer.   Additionally, the 
Company does not have an aggregated picture of non-residential EV charging load. However, 
now that the Company owns charging stations in NY and supported the installation of many 
more through the Phase 1 Electric Transportation Program, it is using this data to support 
new bottom-up load forecasting models. 
Challenges for Widespread EV Adoption: 
National Grid is working to address these three main challenges: 
Education/Awareness:  
Gaps in education and awareness of EV options, lifecycle costs, charging mechanics and more 
all limit adoption. To address these, the company is educating both commercial and

Topic Catalog: 8. Energy Efficiency 
8.1 Introduction 
Energy efficiency (EE) refers to all of the Company’s EE offerings, including those funded 
through the System Benefits Charge (SBC) as well as through base rates.  EE refers to the 
kilowatt-hour not consumed and is considered a distributed energy resource (DER) in New 
York State. 
EE is a critical tool in achieving the energy policy objectives of low-cost energy supply and 
reduced carbon emissions. The Company is a program administrator under the current EE 
programs. The Company is well suited to the role of program administrator with the ability to 
build on existing strong connections with customers and to deliver EE and other demand 
management services that cost less than traditional energy supply.  The Company administers 
its programs alongside the New York State Energy Research & Development Authority 
(NYSERDA), which also has responsibilities to research and develop renewable resources and 
environmental monitoring and protection throughout the State.  The Company expects the 
Commission’s anticipated New Energy New York order will provide further support for 
increasing and accelerating the role of EE in New York’s energy landscape.   
EE is foundational in the Company’s view of the future of the electric grid.  The Company is 
seeing a need for “grid modernization” features such as two-way power flow, active load 
management, DERs, and a focus on consumer education and behavior change supported by 
real-time energy consumption information for customers.  The Company has observed that 
customer interest in ways to be more efficient has increased, and engagement is the first step 
toward customers actively participating in managing their energy use.

Assumptions: 
➢ Additional EE funding and savings targets will be needed to advance the statewide 
goals and National Grid will be assigned a portion of that target; 
➢ Earnings Adjustment Mechanisms (EAMs) or performance-based incentives will 
continue to be used to incentivize cost reductions that allow utilities to achieve or 
surpass their energy savings targets and will be developed during rate cases 
➢ The normal mode of recovery for EE program costs has been to treat them as 
operating expenses, and this will remain the assumption in the absence of a 
compelling demonstration that amortization alternatives are in the ratepayers’ 
interest; 
➢ EE is relied upon in system planning efforts; and 
➢ To meet Company and State goals, the Company may test new tools, technologies, 
offerings and business models through energy efficiency pilot projects. The 
development of such projects may result from Company customer insight and 
strategy work, industry partnerships, technological advancements, and New York 
State policy development. 
8.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customer - EE programs are designed to respond to customers’ needs, improve 
system performance, and reduce overall system electric costs.  The EE programs provide a 
mechanism for customers to reduce their energy usage.  These EE programs encourage 
customers to conserve energy.  In return, overall system reliability and efficiency is 
improved for all National Grid customers.

The Company manages EE as a portfolio, but it delivers EE through distinct programs in

ability to operate its system reliably.

8.5 Challenges: 
 
The Company has been implementing EE programs since 2008 that were aimed at avoiding 
carbon emissions by reducing energy consumption.  While the Company still places a high 
priority on carbon emission reductions, there are challenges to also incorporate additional 
system benefits into EE program strategy.  In some ways, incorporating system benefits can 
minimize the influence of the current and future EE framework. 
 
While EE focuses on reductions in energy usage, the Company is also focused on overall 
demand reduction in order to mitigate traditional utility infrastructure investment.  
Traditional EE measures have ancillary demand savings associated with them.  However, 
using EE to both reduce usage and reduce demand in a significant enough way to avoid 
capital investments requires a strategic realignment of the mix of measures offered by the 
Company.  The challenge is to find measures that have time-differentiated energy savings to 
reduce peak and long measured lives to maintain the system benefits.  The secondary 
challenge will be to incorporate them into the portfolios in a cost-effective way, since 
demand reduction measures are typically more costly and require continuous maintenance. 
 
In order to support the Company and State Energy Plan goals  as well as more localized 
efforts, such as the NYPA Five Cities Energy Plans, it is necessary to increase the rate of 
energy savings year over year.  One of the more significant challenges for the Company is 
identifying ways to meet the State-mandated objectives at reduced costs with improved 
overall value to customers.  In addition, new markets have recently opened that were 
traditionally occupied by NYSERDA.  The Company will look to enter these markets in a cost-
competitive way.

Topic Catalog: 9. Energy Management System, 
Outage Management System, Advanced 
Distribution Management System 
9.1 Introduction 
Energy Management System (EMS) supports transmission and distribution control room 
operators. Field telemetry is gathered and presented to operators for monitoring and 
alarming. Advanced applications support operator decisions, including remote device 
operation. EMS supports control of generators and shares data with transmission owners and 
the balancing authority.  
The Outage Management System (OMS) provides distribution control operators with a 
foundational platform to assess and manage trouble and customer reported incidents on the 
distribution network.  
The Advanced Distribution Management System (ADMS) project is designed to deliver a 
platform solution consisting of a Distribution Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition 
System (DSCADA),advanced distribution applications (DMS), and Outage Management system 
functionality on a common operations platform and network model. The applications are a 
foundational platform that will aid Control Center Operations in managing DERs and 
Advanced Distribution Automation (ADA) for strategic functionality required by the REV 
proceeding and the DSIP filings.   
The Outage Management System (OMS) provides distribution control operators with a 
foundational platform to assess and manage trouble and customer reported incidents on the 
distribution network.

9.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customer - EMS provides the capability to detect changing electrical system 
conditions and to react accordingly. Likewise, EMS supports timely actions by monitoring 
electric system events, presenting alarms to operators, and enabling operators to remotely 
operate devices.  By providing situational awareness, modelling tools, state estimation and 
contingency analysis, EMS also helps system operators make timely and appropriate 
decisions that can prevent outages. 
Electrical system information gathered by EMS is shared with the NYISO, providing critical 
information to secure the transmission system and enabling the ISO, as balancing authority, 
to monitor and control generation. Generator dispatch control signals originating at the 
NYISO are delivered to generators by the EMS.  Control room operators monitor generators 
to ensure generators respond with required generation levels.  EMS is a critical tool used to 
secure the transmission and distribution system and to help preserve the reliability of the 
system.  
The ADMS (DSCADA & DMS/OMS) platform will provide system operators with increased 
situational awareness and thus customer benefits by maintaining reliability as DER 
penetration increases and distribution becomes automated.  The ADMS also provides a 
platform whereby the distribution grid can be optimized creating additional wholesale and 
distribution market efficiencies and enabling increased DER penetration by providing active 
network management capabilities.

communicate with remote devices in substations, generating plants and pole mounted 
devices. Data communicated from remote sites enable operators to receive alarms and

control provided by EMS allows customer outages to be prevented or minimized.  Power

EMS systems are expected to be replaced approximately every ten years.  This replacement

functional and security updates are available and installed. EMS applications and third-party 
software are updated to ensure proper operational capability and security is available and 
vendor support is available.  In system refreshes, servers, network equipment, EMS software, 
operating systems and third-party software are updated.  
Outage Management System:  
The OMS, which is currently operational, provides distribution control operators with a 
foundational platform to assess and manage trouble and customer-reported incidents on the 
distribution network. The application provides both a map-based tool for spatial analysis of 
as well as a detailed tabular listing of outages and incidents.  Key application functionality 
includes predicting location of outages and customer trouble reports, modeling of 
distribution network configuration, coordination of response to 911 calls, and setting of 
estimate time of restoration for customer outages. The system interfaces with the corporate 
GIS for the distribution network model and Customer Information System for customer 
account information and real time trouble reports. The OMS has a separate reporting 
application (FocalPoint) that provides real-time outage-related data to a large community of 
read-only users. The reporting application also stores archived OMS data for historical 
reporting purposes. 
The ADMS project (defined below) will incorporate a phased approach building a base 
platform and upgrading present OMS into a common network model with the DMS and 
SCADA applications, allowing for greater situational awareness and operational efficiencies. 
ADMS Deployment:  
An Advanced Distribution Management System (ADMS) is a group of control room-based 
systems (hardware and software) that allow for greater visibility, situation awareness, and 
optimization of the Company’s electric distribution grid. The overall platform includes 
Distribution Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (DSCADA), an Outage Management 
System (OMS), and advanced applications (DMS). The advanced applications included in the 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 623 of 1030


--- Page 143 ---
Page 142 of 317 
 
system can help the control room operator make more optimal system configuration, 
including DER dispatch, decisions with respect to power aspects of the grid. Applications can 
also automate and centralize distribution functions such as volt-var optimization, and fault 
location/automated restoration. An ADMS will also help to incorporate additional real time 
data into useful solutions from an ever-growing number of field smart devices, DA 
(distribution automation) and DERs (Distributed Energy Resources). It is a critical platform 
for the incorporation and management of DERs and future Distributed System Platform 
(DSP) vision as required by New York’s Reforming the Energy Vision (REV) and supporting 
Distributed System Implementation Plan (DSIP) 
The ADMS project plan will incorporate a phased approach building a base platform and 
upgrading present OMS into a common network model with the DMS applications. A 
separation of the present T&D SCADA system into a Distribution specific SCADA system will 
be part of this phased project and will be integrated on a common platform with ADMS/OMS. 
 
ADMS requirements have been identified and are planned to be delivered in two phases over 
approximately four years. In the first phase, new hardware and software will be deployed to 
host ADMS applications. Outage management will remain in the legacy OMS and distribution 
SCADA will remain in the legacy EMS in phase one. Distribution telemetry will flow from the 
EMS to the phase one ADMS system to enable control room operators to use ADMS 
applications to evaluate potential problems in a monitor and inform manner. This first phase 
of the ADMS will create new operational efficiencies by utilizing baseline applications to 
simulate future states of the network and incorporated distributed energy resources. In 
phase two, additional hardware and software will be deployed to enable distribution SCADA 
to be migrated from the legacy EMS to the ADMS. Outage management functions will be 
deployed in this phase on a common network model with the advanced applications 
delivered in phase 1, creating a cohesive operations platform and enabling the legacy OMS 
to be decommissioned. This phase will enable control room operators to manage and control 
the electric distribution system using ADMS applications. A third phase is envisioned with 
the goal of enabling advanced distribution automation capabilities and active network 
management by integrating with AMI and a DERMS platform supporting DSP.

9.5 Challenges: 
 
The primary challenge for the EMS is to maintain current and secure infrastructure and 
software while maintaining high availability. Historically, the EMS vendor has not 
maintained backwards compatible software, requiring a complete parallel system buildout 
followed by testing and cutover. The Company’s strategy is to apply available software 
updates for a period of approximately seven years, at which time hardware and operating 
systems become increasingly unsupported.  At the seven-year period, a complete 
infrastructure refresh is planned in parallel with an upgrade to the latest major EMS software 
release. 
In horizon 1, there will be challenges associated with building and migrating certain 
functionalities into and out of current and future systems. EMS database, display, and SCADA 
functions will expand to include increased recloser devices and metering associated with 
distributed energy resources. These functions will remain within EMS until the ADMS system 
is tested and deployed. The ADMS project includes a transition of electric distribution SCADA 
from EMS to ADMS and sharing of data between EMS and ADMS via ICCP. A database and 
display migration from EMS to ADMS will be required.  
Another challenge is the adoption of new technologies at the appropriate pace to keep up 
with system needs and the ability to embrace new opportunities (i.e., balancing the

Topic Catalog: 10. Energy Storage 
10.1 Introduction 
Energy storage systems provide a wide range of technological approaches to managing power 
supply in order to create a more reliable grid and potentially bring significant cost savings to 
National Grid’s customers.   With recent interest and advances in the energy storage industry, these 
systems are receiving increased attention from a wide range of stakeholders including utilities, 
end-users, grid system operators, and regulators. The benefits of this emerging technology require 
assessment, quantification, and characterization of specific value propositions to ensure effective 
and efficient integration to the grid moving forward. 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 629 of 1030


--- Page 149 ---
Page 148 of 317 
 
Assumptions: 
➢ The Company works with the NYISO and interested parties to develop a path for 
energy storage assets to participate in wholesale markets, while also providing local 
infrastructure support and system reliability; 
➢ Continued downward trend in the cost of energy storage solutions;  
➢ Energy storage systems (ESS) may also be implemented by customers through the 
New York State Standardized Interconnection Requirements (SIR) process, which 
National Grid has seen a significant increase in applications for energy storage 
projects within its service territory. National Grid anticipates continual increase in 
applications for energy storage in response to the state’s energy storage goal of 1500 
MW by 2025 and 3000 MW by 2030; and 
➢ The Company may own and operate energy storage assets under certain 
circumstances. 
 
10.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customer - ESS has the ability to provide several benefits to the grid that can add 
up to a net benefit for customers. Traditional upgrades are generally passive and provide 
increased capacity, reliability, and/or resiliency, but remain underutilized for the clear 
majority of a given year. Energy storage assets, on the other hand, can provide the same 
benefits, as well as a variety of other benefits during off-peak periods. In addition, the ability 
for ESS to serve localized peak load potentially reduces the need for disruptive construction 
that may otherwise be required for traditional upgrades, and the ability for ESS to participate

10.3 Implementation Plan: 
 
The Company intends to support energy storage resources as a means to improve system 
reliability, assess system improvements, and quantify benefits to customers using data 
obtained from the Company’s system.  The Company will use the BCA tool to estimate the 
value of energy storage in its many different applications. Furthermore, the Company plans 
to update and refine inputs to the BCA tool as new storage sites come online and increasingly 
precise data becomes available.  
National Grid also expects to use this knowledge to investigate possible tariff changes that 
would enable customers to consider market-based incentives for storage, from which grid 
services may then be procured by the Company.  Such tariff changes would likely allow the 
Company to leverage both customer-sited ESS, as well as Company-owned energy storage 
assets, to enhance system performance.  Enabling customers to invest in these technologies 
will reduce the initial capital investment burden on ratepayers, while still leveraging the 
technology to help provide reliable service to a broader group of customers.  The long-term 
goal is for the Company to incorporate the process of identifying and evaluating energy 
storage capabilities (e.g., providing grid services) as a common practice within day-to-day 
operations, much like solar PV is today.  Storage can also  “firm” intermitent power from 
renewable energy resources, thereby increasing the economic benefits and operational

North Troy:  
The North Troy project (formerly the Kenmore project) will test the use of energy storage to 
alleviate an “n-0” distribution constraint at the North Troy substation. The substation 
supplies its 13.2 kV feeders through a single power transformer that is forecasted to surpass 
its normal-rated capacity in the near future. The ESS will be designed to supply energy at 
peak times to reduce the load carried by the station power transformer. This will allow the 
Company to defer replacing the transformer to increase its capacity to serve the area, 
potentially providing cost savings to customers. 
East Pulaski:  
The storage system at the East Pulaski substation is energized and operational to alleviate 
any “n-0” and  “n-1” distribution constraints.  The storage system will relieve loading on the 
single transformer substation where loading is already reaching the rated capacity of its 
transformer under “n-0” system conditions and is working to defer the need for future 
system upgrades. If a failure occurs in the nearby local network, the substation may need to 
supply energy to an increased number of customers, resulting in the possibility of the 
substation surpassing its rated capacity and impacting reliability. This condition has 
occurred, on average, approximately 2.5 times per year and lasted several hours for each 
occurrence.  Over the next couple of years, the Company plans to gain valuable operational 
experience in coordinating the dispatch of the system for local reliability need and 
potentially providing services to NYISO, the state’s bulk system operator.

Towards the end of this period, the Company  expects that the process of identifying and

10.5 Challenges: 
 
The Company’s energy storage program will seek to address the following challenges: 
➢ While costs continue to trend downward, energy storage is still a relatively expensive 
technology. The Company will evaluate the benefits of such systems and focus on 
those that provide positive value. 
➢ Operations and maintenance of energy storage technology is something the Company 
is not yet familiar with.  As such, the Company will continue to develop training and 
education capabilities as ESS is deployed. 
➢ Wholesale market participation is potentially a key energy storage benefit. However, 
the markets have not matured to a place where these assets can easily enter and 
participate. Considerable effort in conjunction with the NYISO, regulators, and 
stakeholders is required as the markets begin to incorporate energy storage. 
➢ Interconnection policies and technical requirements are key for integrating ESS.  The 
Company and various stakeholders made considerable effort the last quarter of 2017 
to establish ESS interconnection process and standards in the SIR for customer 
applications up to 5 MW and continues to be actively engaged in the Interconnection 
Technical Working Group (ITWG) and the Interconnection Policy Working Group 
(IPWG) led by NY Department of Public Service where stakeholders discuss lessons 
learned through implementation of the SIR process. 
➢ New energy storage technologies exist today, with even more likely on the horizon. 
Staying up to date with new developments and understanding niche applications will 
be an ongoing challenge as the industry continues to mature.  
➢ The siting of energy storage, including permitting and local zoning, is a challenge, as 
understanding and comfort with the technology may vary from town to town. In many 
areas where energy storage has not been previously deployed, an in-depth discussion 
is usually required to make local authorities comfortable with the installation of this 
relatively new technology. 
➢ With large scale energy storage reaching increased deployment, revisions to current 
codes, standards, and regulations are playing catchup to the influx of various storage 
technologies.  Keeping current on relevant codes and standards will be a must as 
National Grid continues to evolve and engage in the ESS market.

Topic Catalog: 11. Engineering Reliability Review 
11.1 Introduction 
An Engineering Reliability Review (ERR) is a detailed review of any distribution feeder 
experiencing reliability problems or any localized pocket of poor performance.  ERRs are 
performed on select feeders, defined as Worst Performing Feeders (WPF), as described in the 
Electric Service Reliability Report filed annually in accordance with Case 90-E-1119. 
The scope of an ERR will typically include the following: 
➢ Review of one- and multi-year historical reliability data to identify current issues and 
trends. 
➢ Review of recently completed and/or future planned work which is expected to impact 
reliability. 
➢ Review of the need for the installation of radial and/or loop scheme reclosers. 
➢ Review for additional line fuses to improve the sectionalization of the feeder. 
➢ Comprehensive review of the coordination of the protective devices on the feeder to 
ensure proper operation. 
➢ Review of equipment on the feeder to identify and address equipment in poor 
condition. 
➢ Review of equipment loading on the feeder to identify and address any overloaded 
equipment. 
➢ Review for other feeder improvements such as fault indicators, trip savers, feeder ties, 
capacitor banks, load balancing, additional switches, and potential reconductoring.

distribution feeders that have been identified as WPFs in the annual Reliability Report that 
the Company files with the Commission.  The intent of the ERR is to improve the future 
reliability of these feeders, thereby improving service for customers.

11.3 Implementation Plan: 
 
An ERR of any distribution feeder documents past performance of that distribution feeder, 
evaluates the condition and status of the major equipment on that feeder, includes a 
written document explaining these conditions, and provides recommendations for 
reliability improvements.  The ERR document is broken down into the following sections: 
Section 1:  Historic Reliability Performance/Previous Recommendations 
Section 2:  Line Recloser Installations 
Section 3:  Ratio Transformers 
Section 4:  Additional Circuit Sectionalizing 
Section 5:  Protective Device Coordination Review 
Section 6:  Load Balancing 
Section 7:  Additional Feeder Ties/Feeder Reconfiguration 
Section 8:  System Improvements/System Upgrades 
Section 9:  Feeder Cost Summary 
The tables below are examples from an ERR performed on the Battenkill 34256 feeder. 
Section 1: Historic Reliability Performance/Previous Recommendations:  
A review of the reliability history of the feeder over the past three calendar years is 
performed and a table (as shown below) of reliability indices over that time period is 
provided, listing the number of feeder lockouts and identifying the main drivers of 
interruptions.  The section of the ERR also looks at where the feeder is in the tree trimming 
and I&M cycles and what work identified within these inspections is yet to be completed.  
Finally, it documents any previously identified capital improvement projects that have been 
recently completed or are already scheduled for the future. 
 
Section 2: Line Recloser Installations:  
In this section, all line reclosers on the feeder are identified and a table, similar to the one 
shown below, is provided listing the location of existing reclosers and providing 
recommendations for additional line reclosers where needed.

Section 3: Ratio Transformers:  
A review of all step up and step down (ratio) transformers on the feeder is performed and 
the load on each ratio transformer is estimated.  A relief plan is provided for any ratio 
transformer loaded in excess of 100% of the nameplate rating. 
Section 4: Additional Circuit Sectionalizing:  
This section includes a review of all sectionalizing switches and tap fuses on the feeder and 
makes recommendations for any removals, relocations or additions.  A table would be 
provided listing the number of new fuses and/or switches to be added, removed or changed, 
and with an estimated cost for the changes. 
Section 5: Protective Device Coordination Review:  
A complete review of the coordination of the protective devices on the feeder with the station 
breaker is performed and any recommended changes are identified.  This usually results in 
the addition of fuses on CSP transformers (transformers with internal fuses) and the addition 
of Current Limiting Fuses where needed. 
Section 6: Load Balancing:  
An evaluation of the balance of load between phases is performed, and recommendations 
are provided to address any imbalance seen at the station breaker in excess of 20 percent. 
Section 7: Additional Feeder Ties/Feeder Reconfiguration:  
All existing feeder ties, both three phase and single phase, are identified within this section, 
and recommendations are provided complete with cost estimates for any new recommended 
feeder ties.  
Section 8: System Improvements/System Upgrades:  
Should there be any additional recommendations for reliability improvements that do not 
fall within the previous categories, they will be identified here.  These often include projects 
to rebuild and convert portions of the feeder which are currently served through ratio 
transformers that are not overloaded, projects to relocate rear lot portions of the feeder to 
the road, and the addition of lightning arresters at dead ends or feeder ties. 
Section 9: Feeder Cost Summary:  
A table listing all recommendations is provided which lists the cost of each recommendation 
broken down by Capital, O&M and Removal and includes a total cost for all recommendations

Topic Catalog: 12. Fault Location, Isolation, and 
Service Restoration 
12.1 Introduction 
The Company proposes to deploy Advanced Distribution Automation (ADA) equipment designed 
to accomplish automated Fault Location, Isolation, and Service Restoration (FLISR).  FLISR can 
reduce the impact of interruptions on the distribution system through the installation of 
automated switches along the main line and tie points of a feeder.  This allows a fault to be 
automatically isolated into a sub-section of the feeder and the uninvolved sub-sections to be 
resupplied via automated tie points, significantly reducing both impacted customers and outage 
durations.   The Company currently has communications capabilities on a portion of the reclosers 
on the distribution system but does not currently coordinate their operation during faults 
beyond their local protective control. A FLISR scheme will replace manual tie points between 
adjacent 
feeders 
to 
provide 
downstream 
restoration, 
will 
integrate 
enhanced 
telecommunications and additional control on existing protective switches, and potentially add 
new switch locations as necessary to optimize system reliability.   
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 642 of 1030


--- Page 162 ---
Page 161 of 317 
 
Assumptions: 
➢ The Company continues DSCADA deployment; and 
➢ ADMS development continues. 
 
12.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customers - FLISR deployment will directly help customers served by distribution 
feeders where this technology is deployed.  The Company’s ability to optimally serve these 
customers will be increased due to enhanced situational awareness that comes with 
additional instrumentation points and visibility into the distribution system.  During fault 
conditions, it is expected that a significant reduction in outage minutes will be achieved. 
Optimal feeder re-configuration using the centrally managed FLISR (e.g., ADMS) may be used 
to automatically (with operator consent) change feeder normally open points (typically on a 
seasonal basis) to reduce losses, help mitigate thermal overloads and improve the voltage 
profile.   
In previous years, the Company has implemented a side-tap fusing program to place fuses 
on all high priority side-taps.  Over the past several years, this program has addressed many 
of these side-taps, which will prevent a fault on a side-tap from propagating into a larger 
outage by isolating the immediate area impacted downstream of the fuse.  The Company has 
also been implementing single phase trip savers/reclosers in place of traditional fuses.  
Customers downstream of these trip saver/recloser locations now potentially experience 
only a momentary interruption for what would have been a sustained interruption with 
traditional fusing.  For this reason, the Company is transitioning from the traditional side-
tap fusing program to FLISR and continuing deployments of single phase trip 
savers/reclosers.

performance, cost to deploy, and customers impacted. 
The Company has successfully completed multiple Distribution Automation (DA) schemes 
across Upstate New York service territory.  There are currently two schemes in the Eastern 
region, three in the Central region, and six in the Western region.  The Company’s 
Massachusetts affiliate also completed a similar pilot, referred to as the Worcester Smart 
Energy Solutions Pilot.  These schemes all utilized the S&C Intelliteam Automation platform 
and various type of communications technologies (900MHZ, WiMAX, Cellular). All of these 
pilot projects provided essential feedback and lessons learned to help enable cost-effective 
implementation over the next 15 years. 
New York Pilot – Central Region 2009:  
The central region NY pilot project Sub transmission circuits were activated on January 26, 
2009. The three-year average CMI went from 320,000 to 12,000, and the three-year average 
interruption duration went from 100 minutes to 3 minutes, ultimately resulting in 
cost/benefit ratios better than $10-12/ΔCMI. The results from the pilot project resulted in 
further deployment of Sub-T automation schemes in the upstate New York service territory.

New York Sub-Transmission Distribution Automation Schemes:

12.5 Challenges: 
 
The FLISR program will seek to address several potential challenges as it is deployed: 
➢ National Grid is working through various research projects to review the latest 
FLISR technology. The Company is also looking through various vendors for the 
latest information and methodologies to deploy FLISR schemes. 
 
➢ Determining the most cost effective and technically sound solution for feeder 
communications will be a challenge.  While a combination of private and public 
networks appears to be the best approach at this time, the Company must validate 
this prior to full-scale implementation. 
 
➢ Once an ADMS system is deployed, the Company will need to determine how to 
migrate the FLISR controls to it. 
 
➢ Each year, the Company will refine the selection of feeders for deployment based on 
new data and lessons associated with previous installations. 
 
➢ Integrating DER, particularly DG and energy storage, with FLISR schemes will 
require careful review and may present certain challenges such as coordination of 
protection schemes.  
 
➢ Future proofing the FLISR technology so that the devices (e.g., communication 
modules) can be easily upgraded as new technologies become available will be a 
challenge. 
 
➢ Training the workforce on this new technology (e.g., line workers and operational 
staff) will be required to ensure safe and reliable operation of the FLISR technology.

Topic Catalog: 13. Flood Mitigation 
13.1 Introduction 
Severe storms and flooding in past years have highlighted the potential vulnerability of National 
Grid’s substations. Major flooding events nationwide continue to underscore the importance of 
protecting infrastructure. Emergency response preparation in the Company’s service territory is 
critical.  
In addition to targeted capital projects, the Company has purchased and strategically placed 
extensive amounts of emergency response flood mitigation materials throughout New York State. 
The Company’s field workforces have been trained on the equipment and site-specific action plans 
have been drafted. Engineers and field crews are prepared to respond once notified by the 
Emergency Planning Department.

Topic Catalog: 14. Generator Retirements 
14.1 Introduction 
The Company is trusted with the task of ensuring the transmission system is resilient and reliable.  
This requires planning for the future and making sure system improvements are made prior to 
issues occurring.  As more renewables are added and conventional generating stations reach their 
end-of-life, system dynamics must be reviewed to assure reliability and performance is not 
compromised.  Inertia, which is normally supplied along with power from rotating generators is 
not present with inverters used for renewable generation.  When the available inertia in the 
transmission system is decreased, the frequency change and deviations in the transmission system 
are more likely to cause unexpected tripping, false errors, and protection device malfunction.  
These events can cause system instability and decreased reliability for the transmission system, 
which can cause customers to experience brownouts or blackouts.  And as more existing large 
synchronous generation sources are removed from service, the transmission system will be called 
upon to fulfill locational needs by transferring power over longer distances.  There are a variety of 
technology options to address the future changes in the transmission system, and the Company is 
preparing for this challenge to protect customer reliability. 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 653 of 1030


--- Page 173 ---
Page 172 of 317 
 
Assumptions: 
➢ More non-renewable energy generators will retire between now and 2035 
➢ New technologies to help the electrical transmission system during the retirements 
will be needed 
➢ Smart metering will increase customer choice and interaction 
➢ Impact studies on the transmission system will allow the Company to be proactively 
address anticipated retirements 
➢ Stability and reliability of the transmission system will be the first priorities with 
generation retirements 
➢ New technologies to provide inertia to the transmission system are needed when 
traditional generation sources are retired 
 
14.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customer - With the new Clean Energy Initiatives for New York State, the 
generation sources and locations are expected to change significantly between now and 
2035.  As New York State increases the renewable resource generation, existing fossil fuel 
generation systems can be expected to make economic decisions to shut down.  However, 
the timing of generator retirement decisions is unknown.  Furthermore, there is a possibility 
that such a retirement will adversely impact system reliability and stability.  Stability of the 
electric system has historically been addressed with in service rotational generation.  
Currently, the Company examines its system for potential generation losses in order to 
protect customers from those cost increases by proactively developing generator 
contingency transmission solutions.  The Company, along with other industry experts, will 
continue to monitor stability risks and implement corrective actions when appropriate.
