14.3 Implementation Plan: 
 
Generator Retirement Impact Studies: 
The Company continues to incorporate energy supply assumptions into its generation 
contingency planning cases.  As a result of State and federal policies regarding clean energy, 
the Company anticipates that remaining fossil fuel generators will be the first to retire.  These 
at-risk generators are the first to be reviewed.  Once the energy supply studies are 
completed, the deployment of infrastructure that accounts for multiple system needs (e.g., 
conductor clearance) can be optimized.  Alignment of the Company’s asset management 
strategies, capacity planning needs, and generator contingency plans all aid in prioritizing 
cost-effective transmission upgrade decisions. These proactive strategies and studies will 
enable the system to reliably absorb the loss of a generator due to retirement without the 
need for temporary energy-supply contracts.  Beginning upgrades on the transmission 
system before generator retirements are announced, allows for the transmission system to 
become more resilient. 
Worcester Smart Energy Solutions Pilot: 
The Company’s Massachusetts affiliate is engaged in a smart meter pilot in Worcester, 
Massachusetts.  The smart meters in the pilot provide customers with access to real-time 
electricity rates, usage, and outage information.  This allows customers to control their 
energy usage and, in turn, control their bills.  For example, customers can choose when and 
how to use appliances based on market values of electricity.  The information and technology 
from this pilot will pave the way for the potential implementation of generation choice for 
customers.  Allowing customers another level of choice, such as buying power from certain 
generators, could allow fossil fuel and nuclear generators to be retired and the new 
renewable generation technology to be implemented.  Smart metering capabilities allow

real-time interactions between customer and utility, showing more data on where loading

Battery Energy Storage: 
BES allows for storage and management of power flow for the transmission and distribution 
system.  Taking into consideration the intermittency of renewable generation, the 
implementation of batteries would allow the electric system supply to stabilize, increasing 
generation when supply is low and storing energy when supply is high.  System stability can 
increase with BES because of its capability to store and release power into the system 
instantaneously.  The converter that is in BES may allow for the contribution of reactive 
power to the electric system, taking over for what was lost with retirement of traditional 
rotational generation.  This adds a level of flexibility, resulting in better reliability for 
customers through an environmentally friendly solution.  BES is designed to be placed in any 
environment for ease of use, reducing the number of variables to consider when analyzing 
installation locations. 
Synthetic Inertia: 
Research in the renewables industry has led to the upgrading of wind turbines to allow the 
kinetic energy from the rotating blades to supply a bit more power during a system 
imbalance.  The synthetic inertia that the turbines supply helps to give the transmission 
system what it needs to recover from frequency fluctuations.  Once the frequency is 
stabilized from the kinetic energy, another frequency problem has been shown when 
returning the turbines back to their full speed of generation.  This event can cause protection 
systems to trip and sections of the electric system to be disconnected.  A possibility to combat 
this problem is to put a limit on the power reduction for the turbines.  An estimated 20 
percent reduction of the overall total capacity of the wind turbine should show a smooth 
recovery in the electric system.

14.5 Challenges: 
 
The largest challenge with planning for the retirement of fossil fuel and nuclear generators 
stems from uncertainty in the timing of the retirement.  Market forces, regulations, and 
environmental policies can affect generator economics.  Depending on the specific situation, 
this could lead to accelerated retirement plans or potentially facilitate continued operation 
of an otherwise uneconomic generating unit.  Capital construction projects can be started 
assuming that generation will retire in a certain order, but that is not truly known until a 
generator owner officially announces its intention to retire a unit.  The Company takes the 
position that given the age of the generation fleet in New York, low market prices, and 
shifting environmental regulations, generator contingency planning is based not on “what if” 
planning but “when it happens”.  The Company needs networks that are capable of 
accommodating the loss of such units while managing costs to customers

Topic Catalog: 15. Geographic Information System 
15.1 Introduction 
Geographic Information System (“GIS”) is a geographic-based technology that combines the power 
of maps with the function of a database. The Company utilizes GIS to enable a number of functions.   
For example, the Company uses GIS and associated data as the register for T&D lines and assets, 
the design tool to create distribution plans and estimates, as well as for providing the underlying 
connected model used for processes like Outage Management & Load Flow Analysis.

15.3 Implementation Plan:

The Company has deployed an online GIS-based portal for DER customers and developers to 
access distribution network information, including Hosting Capacity assessments, planned 
projects and other information relevant to the DER community.   Improvements to the portal 
and the data management process are ongoing.   This leverages the GIS-based IMAP platform. 
IOAP Phase II: 
The IOAP has deployed a method to apply for DG interconnection to the electric network.   
The GIS data enhancements are driving accuracy of the automated screens called for in Phase 
II as well as application of geospatial analysis techniques necessary. 
Vegetation Inspection Planning Evaluation Reporting (VIPER) system: 
The Company has developed the VIPER system to support management of the full vegetation 
management program and lifecycle.   This has been deployed for transmission and was 
recently deployed (2019) for distribution.  Leveraging the IMAP platform, the VIPER system 
includes functionality for both office- and field-based workers, allowing for enhanced data 
accuracy, timeliness, and auditability.

Topic Catalog: 16. Hosting Capacity 
16.1 Introduction 
Hosting capacity is defined as the amount of DER that can be accommodated without adversely 
impacting power quality or reliability under existing control configurations and without 
requiring infrastructure upgrades to the primary line voltage and/or secondary network system. 
Hosting capacity automates data analysis and provides visual tools used by both stakeholders and 
utilities to drive decisions and processes.  Primarily, hosting capacity identifies the volume of DER 
that can be accommodated at given locations on the system.  The data analysis from hosting 
capacity can be overlaid on maps to provide customer-centric tools to determine areas that may 
be more or less favorable to DER installations.  Hosting capacity also provides benefits to 
interconnection screening and planning decisions.  
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 666 of 1030


--- Page 186 ---
Page 185 of 317 
 
Assumptions: 
• DER penetrations/applications continue to increase; 
• DER costs will continue to decrease; 
• Customer participation in DER installs will increase; 
• Customer/developer desire for hosting capacity analyses (HCA)/mapping is still 
valid; 
• Grid operators will become more familiar with monitoring and/or operating DER on 
the system (Dispatchable DER); 
• There is a regulatory requirement for Hosting Capacity Analysis (HCA) and mapping; 
• Development of an enhanced version of the Electric Power Research Institute 
(EPRI)’s Distribution Resource Integration and Value Estimation (DRIVE) tool that is 
capable of incorporating the impacts of interconnected DER into sub-feeder-level 
hosting capacity calculations; and 
• National Grid is updating distribution planning criteria to account for increasing 
hosting capacity. 
 
16.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customer - To encourage the widespread growth of DER interconnections, 
developers and customers need up front insight into locations that may require additional 
costs to interconnect their project.  Interactive online maps are created to show a range of 
hosting capacity at the feeder level.  The maps provide developers with early indicators of 
potential costs for a project to see if it aligns with their business models.  Developers combine 
these data points with other information they have gathered to determine which locations 
are best suited for their DER installation projects.   
Hosting capacity can also assist with technical reviews for proposed projects.  Quick, 
accurate technical reviews provide customers information needed to determine the 
feasibility of their projects.  Hosting capacity maps and the underlying data can help utility 
engineers when making decisions on approving a project for interconnection or determining 
that further study is required.

the process of identifying hosting capacity, followed by the second step to increase hosting 
capacity opportunities.

for the implementation of HCA, with each subsequent stage increasing in effectiveness,

The Company completes the HCA by developing feeder models in CYMDIST distribution 
power flow software using the DRIVE software tool developed by EPRI. The DRIVE tool is a 
capacity evaluation application used to determine the ability of a radial distribution feeder 
to host distributed energy resources without causing adverse impacts to the distribution 
system.  The DRIVE tool leverages existing circuit models in a utility’s native distribution 
planning software to carry out an analysis of hosting capacity.  
 
Four-Stage Roadmap to Identify Hosting Capacity 
Stage 1: Distribution Indicators: 
As part of Stage 1, the Company represented a number of hosting capacity indicators on an 
interactive feeder map that presented system data that could prove insightful for potential 
DER hosting.  While true HCA requires detailed load-flow analysis of each feeder, the 
indicators provided knowledgeable viewers with information that could help inform 
expectations about potential DER impact.  The Company also provided additional 
information to guide DER applicants via the System Data Portal, such as a “Red Zone” map 
and “DER Potential Benefits” maps.  The red zones include 5 kV distribution, areas that may 
result in back-feed due the volume of aggregated DG already installed, the number of DG 
applications in the queue, and areas with substations that lack high-side protection (3V0 
protection).  The Stage 1 maps were replaced by the Stage 2/2.1 HCA maps.

Stage 2/2.1: Hosting Capacity Analysis: 
The Company has completed the Stage 2 analysis to provide interactive maps describing the 
gross hosting capacity of each distribution feeder calculated with respect to a large 
centralized solar PV scenario. As part of Stage 2 analysis, the Company evaluated the hosting 
capacity of each feeder on its distribution system using the EPRI DRIVE tool and posted the 
results via an interactive map on the ESRI-based System Data Portal (ESRI is a provider of 
GIS products).  This effort required the development of detailed feeder load flow models and 
an assessment of the impact of DERs along the entire length of the feeder mainline. The range 
of hosting capacity for DER on each feeder is presented as both a heat map as well as with 
tabular data on the interactive map. 
 
Following the initial release of Stage 2 maps, the Joint Utilities worked collaboratively with 
stakeholders to identify additional data elements that could further enhance the value of the

October 1, 2018. Some data elements on the map are updated monthly. The Company 
currently performs yearly HCA on almost 2,000 feeders across its NY service territory. The 
results are currently mapped on the NY system data portal. These maps have been replaced 
on October 1, 2019 with the Stage 3.0 HCA maps.

discussion to be part of a later release is an increased HCA refresh rate than yearly.

Stage 4: Fully Integrated Value and Hosting Evaluations: 
The capabilities in this fourth stage extend beyond the formal definition of HCA and build 
on its foundation to perform fully integrated value assessments. The impacts of DER on 
the electric grid may vary depending on attributes of the DER, the location at which the 
DER is interconnected to the electric grid, and the configuration of the electric network. 
These impacts may be positive or negative; therefore, it is important for utility planners 
to identify the locations where the deployment of DER (or a portfolio of DER) has the 
highest potential to reduce overall net cost of operating the system. The value of DER on 
the distribution system is locational, and may be associated with a particular distribution 
substation, an individual feeder, or a combination of these. 
Value assessments that quantify the full set of benefits from DER require enhanced 
analytical tools and resolution of relevant REV proceedings. The evolution toward this 
type of integrated DER value assessment requires the development of new data, tools, 
methods, and a deeper understanding and characterization of salient value metrics 
driving such analyses. In the longer term, the utilities expect to develop the valuation 
methods and tools necessary for achieving the objectives of this stage. 
Step 2: Increase Hosting Capacity: 
Efforts aimed at increasing hosting capacity are separate and distinct from the HCA, 
where the latter is aimed at enabling the capabilities to develop hosting capacity 
evaluations that inform planning.  These two processes can proceed in parallel and will 
ultimately be informed by one another. Increasing hosting capacity is a topic to be 
evaluated over the next five years. 
There are numerous methods and approaches available to increase hosting capacity 
through strategies, such as DER capabilities, that mitigate limiting factors. Because 
hosting capacity is localized in nature, efforts to increase hosting capacity will also 
have localized impacts. 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 673 of 1030


--- Page 193 ---
Page 192 of 317 
 
The result of a hosting capacity analysis coupled with information regarding the queue 
and results from submitted pre-application reports, utilities and DER developers can 
target areas of the system to increase hosting capacity to allow additional 
interconnection of DER so that system reliability is maintained. While prior 
implementation of utility projects has primarily been focused on addressing existing 
system needs, some have already had the co-benefit of increasing hosting capacity, such 
as voltage conversions, reconductoring, and improving asset information and metering 
data. When these projects fit within a utility’s distribution investment plan and timeline, 
the utility can realize the added benefit of increasing hosting capacity. 
In many cases, a single solution or technology will not be able to address the full range 
of issues (e.g., voltage, thermal, and protection) that can ultimately limit hosting 
capacity. This requires tailoring approaches for increasing hosting capacity to a specific 
location and condition. One example for increasing hosting capacity is the Company’s 
support for advanced inverter functionality, such as frequency and ride through 
functionality or upgradeable firmware for power factor control in order to enable higher 
penetration rates of solar PV technologies. 
Methods for increasing hosting capacity can be described in terms of three broad 
categories: grid-side enhancements, operational changes, and customer solutions.  The 
table below summarizes some methods for increasing hosting capacity.

Methods to Increase Hosting Capacity 
Currently the costs to increase hosting capacity solely for the purpose of DER 
interconnections is borne by the interconnecting entity as part of a Contribution-in-Aid-
of-Construction (“CIAC”) charge in support of a specific interconnection application. 
These upgrades are not implemented proactively by the utility. However, increased 
hosting capacity is often a by-product of many traditional, utility system infrastructure 
upgrade projects. Examples applicable to National Grid include such things as the 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 674 of 1030


--- Page 194 ---
Page 193 of 317 
 
installation of larger transformers and wires, the conversion of distribution from 5kV to 
13kV, or installation of additional voltage regulating equipment. In addition, as the level 
of DER has increased, the Company has revised some of its equipment and design 
standards for new installations to better accommodate the potential for two-way power 
flows. Examples of these revised standards include two-way voltage regulation controls, 
use of switched shunt capacitors instead of fixed capacitors, and the inclusion of 3V0 
protection schemes on all new substations.

based on minimum hosting capacity values for each feeder.

Topic Catalog: 17. Inspection and Maintenance 
17.1 Introduction 
The Inspection and Maintenance (I&M) program is a comprehensive program for overhead and 
underground line assets.  In this program, each asset in the underground and overhead system is 
inspected on a cycle, and inspection results are documented and tracked in a common database.  
These results lead to proactive mitigation of any deficiencies on approved timelines based on the 
severity of the issues. Improvements in the quality of data collection have enhanced the knowledge 
and awareness of field conditions within the system.  Overall, this ensures a positive and proactive 
approach to protect and maintain safe and reliable service by identifying and mitigating risks 
before a failure can occur and impact customers.

➢ New applications will be selected for implementation within the next 10 years; 
and 
➢ New technologies will change inspection trends and policies. 
 
17.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customer - The I&M program is designed to improve safety by inspecting and 
replacing assets prior to failure.  The replacement of damaged or unsafe assets also creates 
a more reliable system.  The I&M program creates a safer and more reliable system for all 
National Grid customers.

17.3 Implementation Plan: 
 
The I&M program drives a consistent inspection approach to benefit customers by 
evaluating asset health and allowing for a safe and reliable infrastructure.  This program is 
intended to meet National Electrical Safety Code (NESC) Section 214, which outlines 
equipment inspection guidelines.   
The elevated voltage program is implemented with annual testing conducted on all utility 
facilities that are capable of conducting electricity and are publicly accessible. Elevated 
voltage testing is performed based on a 1-volt standard to protect the public from exposure. 
 
The inspection program is implemented on a five-year cycle that includes, at a minimum, 
visual examination of towers, poles, guy wires, risers, overhead cables and conductors, 
transformers, breakers, switches, other above ground equipment and facilities, the interior 
of manholes, service boxes, vaults, and other underground structures. The quality assurance 
program ensures compliance with safety standards.  Other implemented inspection 
programs include:  yearly aerial visual and infrared patrol, 10-year wood pole inspection and

Topic Catalog: 18.  ISO-led System Studies 
18.1 Introduction 
As electricity generation and consumption patterns evolve and existing transmission 
infrastructure ages, changes are made to the transmission system to ensure continued system 
reliability. These changes can include the addition of new generation, new infrastructure, and the 
reconfiguration of existing infrastructure. Proposed changes to the transmission system have the 
potential to disrupt the existing balance within the system in a variety of ways, such that system 
reliability is negatively impacted. The Company works closely with the New York Independent 
System Operator (NYISO) as a contributor and collaborator in transmission system studies. These 
studies aim to uncover potential issues with proposed projects during the planning stage, ensuring 
continued system reliability for customers as projects are implemented. 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16)

Assumptions: 
➢ The NYISO will continue to control and operate the Company’s transmission

➢ Retirements of large, centralized generation will increase; and 
➢ Development of DERs and LSRs will increase. 
18.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customer - The NYISO controls and operates all of the Company’s Bulk Electric 
System (BES) assets, as well as a portion of its non-BES assets. It is important that National 
Grid and the NYISO collaborate frequently in order to maintain reliability of high-voltage 
transmission networks. The careful, collaborative planning process of ISO-led system studies 
ensures that potential issues with changes to the transmission system are discovered prior 
to the implementation of those changes. The rectification of any potential issues during the 
planning phase of projects allows customers to benefit from improved system reliability and 
cost efficiency. 
 
Drivers 
Alignment to the driver

Topic Catalog: 19. Line Sensors 
19.1 Introduction 
Line sensors are high accuracy, full power meters that provide detailed information on the status 
and operation of the distribution grid. These devices come in two primary styles: 1) on-the-wire 
style that mounts directly onto distribution conductors; or 2) insulator style that replace crossarm 
insulators and hold the conductors. These sensors can provide valuable operational and planning 
data of the power flow through distribution feeders which can be integrated with existing utility 
systems to better inform analysis for targeted sections of the energy grid. 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 689 of 1030


--- Page 209 ---
Page 208 of 317 
 
Assumptions: 
➢ Line sensors will be needed for data required by other smart grid programs such as 
VVO, CVR, and Advanced Distribution Automation (ADA). 
19.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customers -  Line sensors provide near real-time power measurements  and 
enable engineering and operations personnel to better manage the distribution system, such 
as better voltage optimization strategies to benefit customers.  The sensors also provide 
more accurate data used for hosting capacity calculations, which benefit DG and DER 
providers looking for best-fit locations for their projects.

The sensors are a cost-effective method of

19.3 Implementation Plan: 
 
In order to effectively integrate line sensors into the distribution grid, it is necessary to 
understand the unique capabilities and installation practices of various types of line sensors 
as well as the communication path to be used to bring data collected from the sensor back to 
the Company’s data center.  Sensor measurements will yield near real-time and forensic data 
that will provide deeper insight into system performance as well as monitoring the extent to 
which the grid is nearing its operational limits.  Further use of the data will permit studies 
that will drive design changes for network optimization.  As the Company increasingly uses 
sensor data, data accuracy will increase and fewer assumptions will be required in studies 
such as HCA.  As a result, the Company can provide more precise calculations of hosting 
capacity, which may have the effect of increasing hosting capacity above previously 
identified levels that were based on minimum hosting capacity values for each feeder.  
The Company is currently executing a two-step line sensor implementation plan. The first 
step is to identify key areas of the distribution grid that lack power monitoring and where 
benefits could be derived through its installation. The second step is to deploy the line 
sensors and integrate data measured by the sensor into utility planning and control systems. 
The highest priority for the Company has been targeting areas of the distribution grid 
where there is little or no existing load and/or power monitoring. The Company will 
continue targeting  substations that do not have a Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition 
(SCADA) connection to the Company’s Energy Management System (EMS) and install line 
sensors on the feeder getaways, replicating substation power monitoring functionality.  As 
these substations are upgraded with a Remote Terminal Unit (RTU) and given full SCADA 
connection to EMS, the line sensors can be redeployed in other locations, such as 
bifurcation points in 3-phase mainline, and the high side of stepdown transformers.

Topic Catalog: 20. Large Scale Renewables 
20.1 Introduction 
New York State and Federal clean energy initiatives offer incentives for the development of 
large-scale, transmission-interconnected renewable generation. The development of large-
scale renewables (LSRs) typically coincides with less-developed areas of the grid, as they tend 
to be located in less population-dense areas. Until recently, these lower-voltage local 
transmission networks primarily served distributed loads. With the advent of LSR, these local 
networks must be planned, reinforced, and operated to not only continue serving that 
distributed load, but additionally serve as a generation collection network to transport power 
from widespread renewable development to the bulk transmission system. 
The Company is working to transform Transmission Planning methodologies surrounding the 
study and implementation of LSR interconnections. A holistic study approach ensures cost-
effective interconnection and long-term energy deliverability. These studies pave the way to 
cost effective solutions. The Company seeks to optimize the utilization of the existing 
transmission networks by coupling LSR deliverability with asset condition or reliability 
concerns through Multi-Value Transmission (MVT) solutions. LSRs will additionally be 
supported through the implementation of Non-Wires and New Technology Solutions, such as 
flow control and energy storage, as well as by strategic investment in new transmission 
infrastructure. 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16)

Assumptions: 
➢ New York State and Federal clean energy initiatives will continue to incentivize the

➢ Existing large, centralized fossil-based generation sources will be offset and replaced 
by a growing network of decentralized large-scale renewables; and 
➢ New transmission infrastructure will be needed to provide capacity for 
interconnecting generation rather than to satisfy load 
 
20.2 Drivers:

to both individual customers developers to construct renewable generation sources of 
various sizes, in support of reducing greenhouse gas emissions. As large-scale renewables 
offset and replace existing fossil-based generation, energy prices will be driven down, with 
those saving passed on to customers. The construction of new transmission infrastructure 
and strategic upgrades to existing transmission infrastructure will allow for the effective 
interconnection of these large-scale renewables and, in turn, create a more reliable and 
resilient grid.

20.3 Implementation Plan: 
 
Transmission Planning Methodology Transformation: 
Traditional planning studies focus primarily on system capacity, reliability, and resiliency. 
Previously infrequent generation interconnection requests were studied on a case-by-case 
basis. As LSR interconnections grow in number and size, new approaches to planning studies 
are required to ensure not only continued load-serving capacity, system reliability, and 
resiliency, but additionally ensure the deliverability of existing, proposed, and future 
What
We do
Why

renewable resources. The Company has begun developing a holistic interconnection study 
approach, considering the aggregate effects of numerous proposed LSRs in close proximity 
to ensure the efficient and cost-effective interconnection of these projects, as well as the 
long-term energy deliverability of these projects. 
Multi-Value Transmission (MVT) Solutions: 
Through developing a holistic generation interconnection study approach, the Company 
seeks to find cost effective solutions which realize benefits for project developers, customers, 
and state needs alike. MVT solutions optimize the utilization of the existing transmission 
network by allowing for increased deliverability of LSRs while also addressing asset 
condition or reliability concerns. Consumers receive economic benefits from increased 
injection of renewables. The State benefits from maximizing the utilization of existing and 
planned renewable resources. Customers benefit from advancing the refurbishment of 
degraded assets and improving system reliability. Customers further benefit from avoiding 
the cost of overbuilt or otherwise inefficient solutions which only address individual system 
needs. 
Non-Wires and New Technology Solutions: 
The Company looks beyond wired solutions in delivering power from LSRs. Non-Wires 
solutions such as flow control devices, energy storage, and minor system topology changes 
are evaluated alongside MVT solutions. These non-wires and new technology solutions can 
provide for areas of LSR growth without major system changes. The deployment of large-
scale energy storage is expected to increase as battery storage technologies continue to 
improve and become more economically feasible, allowing for a more flexible grid. 
Transmission Investment for Renewables: 
The Company anticipates a growing need to invest in the construction of new transmission 
infrastructure for the interconnection of LSRs when MVT, non-wires, or new technology 
solutions are not technically or economically feasible. The land-needs of LSRs typically 
leads to their development in non-population-dense areas. The existing local transmission 
networks in these areas were designed to serve relatively little load and often-times may 
not have the capacity to support multiple LSR interconnections. In such cases, investment 
in new transmission infrastructure to replace, supplement, or overlay these existing local 
networks may provide cost savings compared to MVT, non-wires, and new technology 
solutions when delivering power from LSRs.

20.5 Challenges: 
 
➢ The development of LSRs typically coincides with less-developed areas of the grid, 
as they tend to be located in less population-dense areas. Until recently, these 
lower-voltage local transmission networks primarily served distributed loads. 
With the advent of LSR, these local networks must be planned, reinforced, and 
operated to not only continue serving that distributed load, but additionally serve 
as a generation collection network to transport power from widespread renewable 
development to the bulk transmission system. 
➢ The existing ISO interconnection process is focused primarily on the right to 
interconnect, placing the burden of real-time energy deliverability on the 
interconnecting transmission owner. 
➢ Managing power quality and system stability may become increasingly challenging 
as inverter-based LSRs replace large rotating thermal generation, resulting in a 
loss of system inertia. 
➢ Many projects are cost-prohibitive. In some cases, accommodating LSRs may lead 
to a choice between large-scale rebuilds of existing infrastructure on the order of 
10’s to 100’s of circuit-miles, or energy storage on the order of multiple GWh.

Topic Catalog: 21.  Lines Asset Management 
21.1 Introduction 
The Company’s robust planning, design, operation, and maintenance provide a high level of 
reliability to customers.  Asset management for overhead/underground T&D lines plays a key 
role in achieving such highly reliable service.  The Company carefully scrutinizes and chooses 
the equipment it purchases to provide the performance and longevity characteristics required 
for proper operation and protection of the T&D system.  This equipment includes overhead 
conductors, insulators and hardware, line switches, and associated measurement and control 
devices. Since this equipment typically has an expected service life well in excess of 50 years, it 
is critical to choose the right technology from reputable manufacturers.  It is also important that 
the manufacturers have a good track record for supporting the long-life products and making 
improvements that enhance reliability and satisfy the needs of an evolving electric system.

21.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customer - It is important to manage the Company’s transmission and distribution 
line assets on a holistic and strategic basis with the goal of improving electric system 
reliability, power quality, and efficiency for customers.  Therefore, the Company continues 
to investigate ways to improve its asset management practices.  It also seeks to promote 
continual improvement by enabling a common approach to asset management and by 
focusing efforts on the most important issues and opportunities.  At National Grid, asset 
management and engineering are vital to delivering safe, efficient, reliable, and 
environmentally sound performance. By making better use of data, new inspection 
techniques, and improving processes, the Company hopes to improve risk detection, as well 
as operational and replacement strategies. Improved asset management will aid in 
prioritizing asset replacements, minimizing both reliability risk and costs for customers.

Overhead Line Refurbishment: 
In general, the approach for refurbishing overhead lines involves the replacement of 
structures and line components deemed to be in poor condition or failing to meet 
appropriate NESC requirements.  Assets deemed unlikely to perform adequately for at least 
15 years may be replaced when justified by an engineering evaluation and cost 
considerations.  Condition issues are identified through engineering field inspections and, 
when appropriate, materials testing and analysis. For example, samples of older conductors 
may be tested to determine strength and ductility.  Ground line inspection data may also be 
analyzed to determine if the NESC strength requirements are being met. 
If a significant amount of line component replacements are necessary, alternatives to a one-
for-one replacement are examined.  For example, a line upgrade may be considered if 
transmission planning studies show that a system reconfiguration is a better option than a 
straight one-for-one in-kind replacement, or another line might be cost effectively de-
commissioned as a result of the upgrade. 
Conductor Clearance Program: 
In 1914, the NESC first established criteria for the minimum distance required between 
electrical conductors and the ground (conductor phase-to-ground clearance) as well as a 
number of other parameters. Since the NESC design criteria typically undergoes revision and 
updates once every four years, each line constructed by National Grid meets different 
versions of the NESC standards.  The applicable code at the time of construction is considered 
the ‘governing code’ for the design criteria.  The 2012 NESC is the current governing code for 
new transmission lines located in New York. 
Asset Management Standard (AMS):  
National Grid approved a new Asset Management and Engineering Standard in 2017 that 
lays out requirements for asset strategy and planning, life cycle delivery, and risk and review.  
An internal and external  team of subject-matter experts was formed to oversee the 
implementation of the standard for the electric side of the business, and will include asset 
management training, a maturity assessment, and the development of an asset health 
scorecard.  The standard will provide a framework for continually improving the Company 
asset management practice based on internationally recognized best practices.  The effort 
will benefit National Grid customers by improving the timing of asset replacements to 
restrain costs and bolster system integrity and reliability. See Topic Section 2 – Asset 
Maturity for more details on Asset Maturity Strategy. 
AMS touches many parts of National Grid: 
➢ Human resources may work with the AMS to develop competency models, training 
programs, and processes for coaching and mentoring;

EPRI Program 37 – Substations: 
National Grid participates in specific EPRI Program 37 projects: 
➢ P37.108: Gas Insulated Substations and Lines – Gas insulated substations and gas 
insulated lines offer many benefits including physical security, compact size, 
modularity, and protection from harsh environments.  They also present challenges, 
including higher initial costs, maintenance issues, and potential leakage of SF6 (a 
powerful greenhouse gas).  EPRI’s Research and Development department is helping 
utilities reduce maintenance costs and uncertainties, minimize SF6 emissions, and 
improve life-cycle management of gas insulated substations and lines through the 
following: 
o Researching and demonstrating effective methods for on-line diagnostics of 
gas insulated substations and gas insulated lines; and 
o Researching the performance of SF6 replacements, starting first in gas 
insulated substations and lines bus since there is no arc interruption.  Once 
this step is successful, further research will extend to gas insulated substation 
chambers that experience arcing (breakers, disconnectors, grounding 
switches). 
➢ P37.114: Physical Security & Intentional Electromagnetic Interference – This 
research develops an understanding of the effectiveness of response options to 
physical security and intentional electromagnetic interference events to reduce the 
potential of transmission and substation asset damage, while also enhancing 
resiliency. 
o Potential intentional attacks against electric power systems include sabotage, 
physical assault and destruction, disruption of sensors, information systems, 
and computer networks, tampering with process safety, disruption of fail-safe 
systems, and indirect attacks, such as the disruption of water, fuel, or key 
personnel. Hundreds of attacks against substations have been conducted 
around the world in the last decade 
o While this project primarily focuses on issues at the transmission line 
substation level, most of the findings are applicable to other areas, such as 
distribution and generation assets.

reliability standards. New aluminum conductor composite reinforced options are available

LineCore, a corrosion detector for conductors, assesses the condition of the galvanic 
protection on transmission line aluminum conductor steel reinforced conductor and 
overhead steel shield wires by accurately measuring the thickness of the zinc layer across 
an entire span, detecting anomalies caused by corrosion without taking samples of 
conductor, which requires consequent splicing. The data obtained by LineCore can be used 
to calculate conductor degradation and help evaluate its remaining service life. The 
technology, a robotic device with non-destructive sensors, is able to negotiate most line 
obstacles and allows for access to hard-to-reach segments such as spans in mountainous or 
agricultural regions and water, highway crossings, and railroad crossings. In addition to 
inspection, LineCore can also safely perform certain maintenance tasks such as repairing 
broken conductor strands.

Topic Catalog: 22. Load, DER Forecasting and 
Planning 
22.1 Introduction 
The Company envisions establishing a comprehensive unified simulation environment that 
provides a spatial and temporal view of load and DER growth, in order to support planning, 
energy procurement, customer engagement, operations, system processes, asset management, 
and efficient energy utilization optimization.   
This approach entails developing: 1) detailed power-flow models for feeder circuits, including 
models of secondary circuits and each individual customer; 2) probabilistic and predictive hourly 
load shape models; and 3) predictive models for future DER installations.   
Essentially, this would allow the Company to produce a forecast at any level of the distribution 
system from the individual customer level up to the feeder, the substation, and the transmission 
system.

Moreover, transforming the forecasting paradigm from traditional statistical relationships

22.3 Implementation Plan: 
 
Forecasting: 
Forecasting must transition to more advanced methods that can predict customer activities, 
behaviors, and decisions, and their impacts on the existing and potential future system, 
instead of simply describing the end result of them in terms of load. This transition makes 
forecasting more dynamic, ultimately leading to a tighter coordination between T&D 
planning and forecasting, resulting in more effective system plans. 
 
The Company has developed a multifaceted forecasting approach with regard to its DER 
growth models.  This approach is comprised of two forecasting methodologies that are 
modeled independently and then integrated utilizing an adjustment methodology to form a 
consistent view.  The methodologies are: 
1. System Level: econometric and growth models 
2. Feeder-Level: customer-specific load and DER growth models 
System Level: Econometric and Growth Models: 
The forecasts derived by these types of models are driven by historical and future economic 
and policy considerations that assume relationships between economic and load growth will 
continue, notwithstanding the impacts of lowered load over time due to the success of DERs 
(or in the case of beneficial electrification, higher loads).  In the shorter term, they expect a 
continuation of near-term program goals and trends. In the longer term, they assume that 
market conditions will materialize to enable most policy-based technology, and program, 
state, and regional goals will be met.   System level forecasts are high level, typically at the 
Company, ISO zone, and transmission planning areas levels but  do not account for the 
heterogeneity of individual customers or diversity of load impacts at the distribution system. 
They instead group customers into typical revenue classes including residential, commercial, 
and industrial.  The output of an econometric growth model is generally statistically-based.  
System level forecast models are efficient to build and are valuable in ensuring that the 
broader aggregate market trends and load changes are captured.  They also provide the 
necessary boundaries and adjustment targets for the next step. 
Feeder Level: Customer-Specific Load and DER Growth Models: 
System Level perspective is valuable for incorporating overall state policies and market 
drivers and has been utilized for overall system planning. However, the accelerated increase 
in the number of DERs across the system has necessitated the need for more granular, 
spatially- and temporally-oriented forecasts. Therefore, more specific forecasts at the 
distribution feeder and substation levels are warranted. In addition to the Company needs, 
the New York State Public Service Commission (PSC) recognized this as well and launched

Implementation Plans (DSIP) for each of the electric utilities. Therefore, the Company plans 
to integrate forecasts with a higher temporal and geospatial granularity that encompass an 
increasing number of variables into planning and associated feeder models to more 
accurately reflect DER impacts. Feeder Level forecasting begins with modeling base load and 
DERs at the customer level for each customer and then maps each customer load model into 
specific feeders in the distribution system model developed in a simulation platform. This 
forecast utilizes the Bottom-up approach which considers detailed customer-level 
information, and models are built for customers with regard to load and DER.  The output 
from the customer models is then aggregated to the feeder level. These models are more 
complex to build due to the volume of models and detailed data required, but they are 
necessary to account for the complexity and heterogeneity in both the system and the 
customer base.  These models can be more accurate because they take into consideration the 
entire load shapes of each individual customer and DER element. The Company has 
overcome the computational complexity of this type of model with cloud computing. 
System Level and Feeder level forecasts by themselves are independent and separate 
forecasts that can/will yield different results.  In order to make sense of the different views, 
the two forms of forecasts need to be unified.  This reconciliation process takes place in the 
adjustment process.  
 
A probabilistic load forecast will likely be developed and delivered over the 5, 10, and 15-
year time horizons.  At the foundation of the forecast will be the creation of 8760 load profiles 
that are created utilizing both the top-down and bottom-up methodologies that were 
previously described.   
Bottom-up load profiles will be created for: 
1. Base load 
2. Load or supply driven by each new DER component 
Modeling DER utilizing the DER model framework will also enable the disaggregation of DER 
so that the load growth of all load contributing components of DER can be understood.  
Coincident load profiles may be available for the following supply and load contributing DER 
components:

Topic Catalog: 23. Microgrid 
23.1 Introduction 
A microgrid (MG) is a group of interconnected loads and DERs within clearly defined electrical 
boundaries that acts as a single controllable entity with respect to the grid. A MG can connect and 
disconnect from the grid to enable it to operate in both grid-connected or island mode. MGs are well 
suited to areas that have existing DER assets, and areas requiring a higher level of reliability and 
resiliency. 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 715 of 1030


--- Page 235 ---
Page 234 of 317 
 
Assumptions: 
➢ Extreme weather events will continue to impact New York; 
➢ Policies and standards will help to enable faster, safer, and more reliable MG designs; 
➢ DER costs will continue to decrease; 
➢ Customer participation in MGs will increase; 
➢ MGs will eventually be driven by market pricing; 
➢ Grid operators will become comfortable with MG operation; 
➢ MG demonstrations will be successful; and 
➢ Public policies will continue to promote MGs. 
23.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customers – Microgrids (MGs) provide a number of benefits to National Grid’s 
customers.35 Customers connected to the MG (often high priority customers, e.g., emergency 
services) receive high reliability and resiliency. Resiliency means customers remain 
energized even in the most extreme circumstances (e.g., hurricanes, ice storms, and grid-
scale blackouts), maintaining essential services and potentially saving lives.  Customers often 
play a central role in the MG system by providing energy from behind the meter DERs such 
as Combined Heat and Power (CHP) and/or participating in DR.  Through participation 
customers can receive financial incentives in return.  MGs may be able to offset traditional 
wires-based solutions if they are located in areas of system constraint, providing more value 
to customers.

able to integrate any DER technology and may 
increase their benefits by encouraging DERs to 
connect to areas where they are most needed.

23.5 Challenges: 
 
Going forward the Company plans to address a number of MG challenges in the areas of 
financial model and ownership, regulatory and legal, operational control and reliability 
needs, customer interaction, and engagement.  
As customers play a central role in MGs, understanding customers’ changing needs, desires, 
and benefits will need to be continuously monitored.  
Due to the inherent complexity of MGs it will be crucial to define ownership, operational 
control and financial models and communicate those models to all stakeholders.  These 
models will need to identify cost disbursement according to those who benefit.  
Transitioning between the various MG modes (grid-island, island, and island-grid), the 
associated controls and protection schemes need to be well defined, simulated, tested and 
demonstrated.  As MGs are complex in nature, time to develop and build out these systems 
will continue to be challenging. The Company plans to identify areas to streamline MG 
project timelines, leveraging national standards currently under development such as the 
IEEE P2030 and 1547 series of standards and guides.   Further development of the 
Company’s ESB 756 from the results of the Interconnection Policy Working Group and the 
Interconnection Technical Working Group will be instrumental in the interconnection 
process of MGs.

Topic Catalog: 24. NERC / NPCC / NESC Requirements 
24.1 Introduction 
National Grid’s operations are governed by a variety of national and regional standards and 
regulations, such as those set forth by the North American Electric Reliability Corporation 
(NERC), the Northeast Power Coordinating Council (NPCC), and the National Electric Safety 
Code (NESC). One way in which the Company meets or exceeds these standards is by 
continually studying, developing, and implementing improvements to its transmission system. 
These improvements include a wide range of work such as substation upgrades, line upgrades 
and replacements, protective relay replacement, and security upgrades. All of the system 
improvements are tied together by overarching goals of increasing safety and system 
reliability, which in turn benefits National Grid’s customers. 
In support of the development of physical improvements to the transmission system, there are 
numerous planning processes which are also aimed at addressing system reliability. The 
importance of this work is highlighted by a collection of standards and regulations which 
ensure that transmission owners and operators offer great consideration to the wide range of 
factors which affect system reliability.

Cybersecurity and physical security are major areas of focus in

24.3 Implementation Plan: 
 
Conductor Clearance Program – NY:  
The Company maintains overhead transmission line clearance information from aerial 
surveys which is used to calculate line sag.  As more current flows through a line, the line’s 
temperature increases.  With increased temperatures, the line stretches and sags.  The 
allowable line sag is dictated by applicable safety codes.  Line sag is used to establish 
maximum allowable conductor temperatures, which in turn are used to determine 
conductor limits for transmission power flow ratings.  The purpose of the Company’s 
conductor clearance program is to ensure the safe operation of transmission lines so as to 
provide reliable service and safe conditions for customers.  In cases where line ratings are 
reduced significantly due to clearance issues, physical changes may be made to the section 
of line in question, or system changes may be made to reduce loading on the line in question. 
This program also has the added benefit of addressing aging infrastructure where 
appropriate and makes the networks more resilient.   
Transmission Substation Physical Security Program: 
The transmission substation physical security program is driven by the need for additional 
physical security measures at certain substations to mitigate break-ins and the increasing 
risk that unauthorized access may lead to potential injury or death of a trespasser who comes 
in contact with energized equipment. Reducing and detecting unauthorized access also 
reduces the risk of vandalism and damage to electric system equipment and increases 
protection against physical attack to transmission stations.  The projects add physical 
security measures that comply with NERC standards, and ultimately provide security to 
prevent loss of power to customers.

Substation Upgrades and Rebuilds: 
Substation equipment upgrades, or complete substation rebuilds may be necessary to 
comply with applicable standards and regulations. This may be due to changes in standards 
and regulations, equipment condition concerns, or significant changes to the transmission 
system which require major reconfiguration of a substation. These upgrade standards are 
set in place to ensure the resiliency of the transmission system and prevent interruptions in 
meeting customer demand. This program has the added benefit of removing hazardous 
materials and environmentally unfriendly liquids from the premises.

Topic Catalog: 25. Non-Wires Alternatives 
25.1 Introduction 
Non-Wires Alternatives (NWAs) are electric system investments and operating practices that can 
defer or replace the need for traditional utility investments for wires-based transmission and/or 
distribution projects.  Successful NWAs produce system-wide benefits when compared to an 
avoided traditional wires project which are quantifiable in terms of a Benefit Cost Analysis (BCA) 
performed by the Company.  NWA opportunities are determined through system planning 
techniques that identify geographical areas that require grid improvements such as reliability and 
system capacity. Common NWA technologies include dynamic load management (DLM), 
distributed generation (DG), energy efficiency (EE) and energy storage systems (ESS). 
 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 729 of 1030


--- Page 249 ---
Page 248 of 317 
 
Assumptions: 
➢ The DSP market and the value of DER (VDER) proceeding will continue to evolve, 
driving value for DERs; 
➢ NWA solutions perform as expected; and 
➢ NWA solutions are cost effective and continue a downward trend in price compared 
with traditional solutions. 
 
25.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customer - NWAs support system needs and reduce overall system electric costs 
for customers by providing an alternative to traditional utility investments.  Viable NWAs 
maintain or improve customer reliability for less than a traditional solution, when 
accounting for benefits from system production costs and emissions. NWAs provide the 
opportunity for customers to participate in the solution (e.g., through DR) and receive 
savings/payments in return.  The Company’s experience with targeted deployment of NWAs 
should help identify opportunities for NWAs as part of a more robust system plan.

Topic Catalog: 26. Operational Telecommunication 
Modernization 
26.1 Introduction 
As the Company looks across the various technologies that enable grid efficiency, market 
animation, greening the grid, and a resilient grid, a few foundational elements need to be in place 
for the technologies to be effective. One of these elements is a robust and secure operational 
telecommunications network. As innovation growth in the industry continues, the Company 
must anticipate the need for connectivity and communications.  At the same time, Verizon will 
be phasing out analog-leased circuits used by the Company for high-speed relay and protection 
systems on transmission lines.   The Company has seen increases in monthly recurring costs and 
a steady decline in services for these analog circuits.   The Company recognizes the importance 
of a reliable communications infrastructure.  The ambition is to leverage the Operational 
Telecommunication Modernization (OpTel) project outcomes, by seeking to create a forward-
looking operational telecommunication strategy to replace the reactive, project-specific model 
that exists today.  Evolution of the Company’s operational telecommunication network and 
governance is needed to cost effectively meet changing customer needs and to protect, control, 
and monitor assets in the future.

➢ Operational telecommunications and communications remain foundational 
elements to grid modernization activities. 
26.2. Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customer - Upgrade of analog communication circuits is consistent with the 
Company’s goal of improving reliability across the system.  Private, dedicated circuits that 
provide time certainty in signal speeds are necessary to ensure the reliability and security of 
the electric transmission grid.  Multiple tiers of modernizations will affect improved 
communications performance, which will enable enhanced system reliability, quicker 
restoration, and provide customers with more timely information, allowing for more energy 
choices.

26.3 Implementation Plan: 
 
The Company will start migrating analog protection circuits to its own private 
fiber/microwave networks to maintain protection and communication needs of the 
transmission system.  Verizon has been unable to provide a definite phase out schedule of 
the existing circuits.  However, based on industry experience, the phase out is expected to 
accelerate.  Historically, Verizon customers had approximately 18 to 24 months to migrate 
the circuits after Verizon announced phase out plans, but the Company anticipates this will  
occur at a faster pace in the future.  A solution proposed by Verizon to convert analog to 
digital circuits does not include all of the communications requirements outlined by National 
Grid’s Protection Engineering department to meet the needs of the electric transmission 
system.  Furthermore, Verizon fiber is not available everywhere.  As such, some Company 
substations would not have access to Verizon fiber, giving rise to other solutions, such as a 
Company-owned private/microwave network. 
OpTel modernization will be deployed in components, organized by stacks of network 
“tiers.” Tier 1 is the core network backbone of redundant private fiber and redundant private 
licensed microwave. Tier 2 is the mid-tier backhaul network of private fiber, private licensed 
microwave, or private licensed Point to Multi-Point at 3.5GHz/5GHz. The Company has started 
the OpTel Asset Inventory project that also contains a new tool for planning, engineering, 
design of new and existing communications.  It is expected that this project will be completed 
sometime in the fall of 2020. 
The Company intends to deploy Tier 1 and Tier 2 network modernization initiatives starting 
in 2018. These include addressing critical and key facilities, replacing analog SCADA 
equipment to avoid obsolescence, and deploying fiber for teleprotection services. The 
Company has started analysis to determine the best replacement equipment for our SONET network 
and should be completed in mid-2020.  This equipment decision will allow us to progress to the next 
stage of replacing of the SONET End-Of-Life Equipment Refresh and other tier 1/2 projects. 
Tier 3 is the field area network of licensed sub 1GHz Point to Multi-Point wireless 
connectivity for the Company’s mobile workforce, distributed automation for SCADA, and 
customer substation connectivity.  
The Company plans to deploy mobile workforce, operational voice and data modernization 
initiatives 2019-2026, including land mobile radio upgrade and private Voice over Internet 
Protocol (VoIP) upgrades. 
Tier 3 network modernization initiatives should be deployed from 2020-2030. These include 
delivering on REV objectives, upgrading Gas Gate regulators, replacing existing capacitor 
“cap” banks & reclosers, and upgrading connectivity to key customer substations. These 
support Tier 4 applications, which are the home area network of Internet of Things (IoT)-
networked devices, DR, DERs, and other home management systems.

Topic Catalog: 27. Outdoor Lighting 
27.1 Introduction 
The Company’s Outdoor Lighting business represents a customer centric, service-oriented 
unmetered electric business segment addressing outdoor lighting, traffic signal and ancillary 
attachment facilities that are either installed, owned and maintained by the Company or 
through a ownership/maintenance/billing matrix between the customer and the 
Company.  The former utility-owned street lighting paradigm is experiencing an extensive 
transformation in the northeast caused by various external initiatives.  These include: 
➢ the adoption of federal and state legislative and regulatory mandates effecting 
ownership, occupation access, energy billing and cost recovery; 
➢ energy efficient light emitting diode (LED) technology in parallel with the advent and 
deployment of wireless control and metering technologies; 
➢ diverse “smart city” attachment technologies; 
➢ expansive deployment of advancing 4G LTE and 5G wireless communication 
technologies; and 
➢ subsidized funding for customers to rapidly facilitate these technologies. 
The Outdoor Lighting paradigm shift has significantly impacted the Company’s established 
business policies, practices, standards, information systems and organization. The prospective 
business changes that are envisioned include tariff provisions and rates which proactively 
address and properly compensate the Company, an organization tailored to meet the needs of 
the altered business model, information systems which promote efficient business 
management and billing processes and the adoption of wireless metering technology 
incorporating advanced location depiction and asset management functionality. 
Exhibit__(EIOP-16) 
Page 747 of 1030


--- Page 267 ---
Page 266 of 317 
 
Assumptions: 
➢ Transformational change to a customer-centric lighting and attachment business 
model. 
➢ Widespread adoption of network lighting control and other smart city technology in 
6-8 years. 
27.2 Drivers: 
 
Focus on Customer – Legislative and regulatory initiatives are driving the Outdoor Lighting 
business to strategically restructure to focus on the administrative management of 
unmetered energy consumption of an ever-increasing population of customer-owned street 
lighting and ancillary attachments.  The Company continues to investigate and adopt 
advancing technologies and innovative regulatory programs to address continuous 
enhancements to benefit customers’ lighting services, promote positive environmental 
change and provide financially beneficial solutions.

Topic Catalog: 28. Protective Relay Updates 
28.1 Introduction 
Protective relaying is used to isolate, or “clear,” a fault from the transmission system in as short 
a time as possible to prevent the effects of the fault from spreading throughout the system. 
These protective relaying systems are custom-tailored to the topology of the transmission 
system. When changes are made to the system topology, corresponding adjustments must be 
made to the protective relaying systems to ensure continued or improved system resiliency 
and reliability for customers. 
Telecommunication capabilities are vital to the effectiveness of the protective relaying systems. 
Currently, the Company relies primarily on analog leased circuits to facilitate this 
telecommunication need. These lines are in the process of being phased out, and there is no 
adequate replacement from providers. This has resulted in the idea of using a Company-owned, 
private digital network. The implementation of such a network would benefit customers 
through improved system reliability by updating and upgrading the existing infrastructure. It 
would also reduce long-term costs, as the new network would be owned, operated, and 
maintained by the Company rather than leased from a provider.

28.3 Implementation Plan: 
 
Relay Replacements: 
Electromechanical relays which are used in the protective relaying system are critical 
components for the rapid isolation of faults on a significant portion of the transmission 
system. They serve to protect customers from outages and protect infrastructure from 
damage. These relays have a limited usable lifespan, after which they must be replaced due 
to condition concerns, performance issues, obsolescence, or as determined by regulatory 
What
We do
Why
We do it
How

Future
Road Map

criteria. These electromechanical relays typically come with a 15-year warranty. After that 
15-year period, manufacturer repair of the relays becomes costly, and it can often be more 
cost effective to simply replace them. The Company plans to continue replacing the worst 
6% of its existing relays over the next 5 years (FY20 – 25). After this time, pilot replacement 
programs will allow for the study of efficient, cost effective replacement of the remainder of 
the relay population. 
Upgrade Communications Equipment Due to Verizon Retirements: 
Verizon will be phasing out analog leased circuits used by the Company for the protection of 
its transmission lines. The Company is planning to transition these analog protection circuits 
to digital DS1 circuits and/or private fiber/microwave networks to maintain protection and 
communication needs.  Upgrade of analog communication circuits is consistent with the 
Company’s goal of improving reliability across the system. Digital circuits enhance disaster 
recovery abilities, allowing communication circuits to be restored and rerouted faster during 
outages. 
Fiber Optic Static Lines: 
One cost-effective method for implementing a company-owned private fiber network is the 
installation of fiber optic static lines. Static lines are the smaller conductors at the top of 
transmission line arrangements. They are used to conduct lightning strikes to ground so that 
lightning does not strike the active conductors. A fiber optic static line is a static line which 
has fiber optic communication lines incorporated into the metal conductor. This allows for 
communication signals to be run between substations. The Company has installed several of 
these fiber optic static lines in pilot programs. Additional installations of these fiber optic 
static lines may allow for the development of a Company-owned private network. 
Adaptive Relaying: 
Adaptive relaying is a current area of research in the field of protective relaying. Adaptive 
relaying allows the protective relaying system to dynamically adjust its settings based on 
real-time system conditions. This technology has the potential to further improve the speed 
with which the system responds to a fault on a transmission line, as well as the potential to 
increase usable system capacity. The Company will begin pilot programs as this technology 
is further developed and begins to become technologically and economically feasible for 
implementation. 
Transmission Ground Fault Overvoltage Protection: 
The increase of DER resulting in backfeed through substation transformers requires 
assurance that the transmission system is protected from ground fault overvoltage (GFOV) 
events.  Optical technologies to detect voltages on the transmission side of power 
transformers are being evaluated by the Company for efficient and economic 3V0 protection 
system solutions.

28.5 Challenges: 
 
➢ Decentralization of generation and increases in inverter-based generation, such as 
renewables, leads to difficulties in detecting faults. This problem results from lower 
values of fault current into the system from the inverter-based generation.  Difficulty 
detecting faults can lead to system instability and damage to infrastructure. 
Protective relay-based solutions to this issue are currently only an area of research in 
the power industry. 
 
➢ The timeframe of the analog leased line phase out is currently unknown, making it 
difficult to develop a timeframe for the rollout of the private digital network. 
 
➢ The existing electromechanical protection relays are from a variety of manufacturers 
and rely on a variety of different communication systems. It is thus a difficult task to 
implement a system-wide upgrade without the completion of the pilot programs.

Topic Catalog: 29. Storm Hardening 
29.1 Introduction 
The Company’s storm hardening program addresses the resilience of the delivery system in select 
areas of its service territory that have experienced repeated outages during adverse weather. The 
Company’s effort improves reliability and customer satisfaction in areas that experience multiple 
storm-related interruptions. The storm hardening program includes reconductoring with tree 
resistant conductors, increase pole size where appropriate, and the use of Grade B construction on 
critical poles and road/rail/water crossings.  In addition, the Company considers new 
sectionalizing points, enhanced lightning protection, and enhanced vegetation management as part 
of its storm hardening efforts.

Next generation materials 
Transmission has proactively transitioned from using 
solid 
round 
wood 
poles 
to 
direct-embedded 
galvanized steel whenever possible.  The use of steel 
eliminates the threat posed by wood peckers, insects 
like carpenter ants, and decay.  Reliability and 
resiliency will improve over time.  Round wood poles 
may have to be used in the interim as direct embedded 
steel pole inventories are built for standard 
configurations. 
Transmission has also transitioned to toughened glass 
insulators (TGI).  TGI are lighter and over time do not 
lose their finish like porcelain insulators do.  This 
allows the shedding of contaminates for a longer 
duration.

Overhead Distribution Standards: 
The National Grid Overhead Distribution Standards specifically address storm-hardening 
protocols.  Storm hardening content in the Overhead Distribution Standards is based on a 
research partnership with EPRI. The standard covers rebuilding of existing infrastructure 
and all new construction.  These standards apply to new customer services, inspection and 
maintenance replacements, damaged equipment replacement, asset replacement, and load 
relief projects.     
Transmission System Resiliency: 
The frequency and severity of extreme weather 
events in New York has disrupted power for 
dozens of communities over the past number of 
years.  Storms cause considerable damage to 
electric system infrastructure, 
potentially 
leaving hundreds of thousands of customers 
without power. 
 
Electric utilities are responsible for the 
reliability of their systems and planning the 
power needs of their customers. With the 
construction of the National Grid transmission 
system beginning in the early 1900s, the 
system has a wide age variance of transmission 
lines and substations. In addition to ensuring 
the Company has the right amount of resources 
to properly maintain its networks, including 
outage restoration efforts, it must seek to 
harden 
infrastructure 
to 
make 
it 
less 
susceptible to climate change.   
 
Even though there is growing concern and 
evidence over the critical need for enhanced 
system resiliency, there is no standardized 
framework for assessing the system resiliency. 
National Grid has adopted the EPRI model of 
Resiliency for its Transmission System.  This 
model focuses on three aspects of Resiliency; 
Damage Prevention, System Recovery and 
Survivability. 
While high-impact, low-frequency events are 
not preventable, the goal of a storm-based

resiliency strategy is to limit the impacts on customers, reduce the Company’s exposure to 
risk, and minimize associated costs. One important aspect of mitigating the risk from 
frequent stronger storms is the identification of resulting outage severity caused by likely 
asset failures.  If after the risk of a storm-related outage event is identified and deemed 
unacceptable, then the Company should be able to manage that risk through one or a 
combination of Damage Prevention, Recovery, and Survivability. 
The process the Company will employ to measure the transmission system resiliency is to 
assess the system vulnerabilities in terms of load at risk due to the loss of a single 
transmission element. This can be further evaluated in terms of customer impacts by 
collaborating with the Transmission Control Center (e.g., number of customers interrupted 
and potential outage duration). Assumed equipment damage, likelihood of failure, and 
repair/restoration process will also be assessed to identify applicable cost-effectiveness 
mitigation solutions (“countermeasures”). 
In New York steps have been taken to protect critical transmission infrastructure against 
some severe weather events. For example, several projects have recently been initiated to 
mitigate the flooding risks at critical substations and going forward flood mitigation is 
intended to be a design criterion for all transmission stations. The Company also has a spare 
equipment strategy which allows it to respond quickly with the appropriate equipment if 
there is limited damage to the system.  From a maintenance standpoint, National Grid 
routinely performs maintenance and replaces degraded assets as a “storm hardening 
activity”, albeit the primary replacement consideration is asset condition and not resiliency.  
Simply said, National Grid strives to maintain its assets and networks to the criteria under 
which they were built, but most of the Company’s assets and networks may not have been 
designed to withstand today’s climate. 
Despite current actions taken, sections of National Grids networks are very old and were not 
designed with an eye towards mitigating the full effects of the growing frequency and power 
of storms. There are but a few standalone projects that are designed specifically to address 
storm related impacts. However, it is unclear on how to accurately quantify the absolute 
resiliency of our network and storm related risks. 
Distribution Grid Resiliency Research Program: 
National Grid’s Distribution Grid Resiliency Research program conducted with EPRI took a 
look at a wide range of resiliency issues, including storm hardening.  The recently completed 
project investigated ways to make lines and structures survive major storm events and ways 
to make lines and structures fail in predictable and more easily repairable ways.  Much of 
this work looked at how falling trees affect lines and structures and how to mitigate or 
control the resulting failures.  Continuing work at EPRI (additional work identified at the end 
of the original three-year project) is looking at ways to control failures from tree impact 
loads such as how to make components that are easier to repair be the ones that fail first.

and determine direction of the program going forward.  The revised storm-hardening 
construction standards will continue to overlap with other programs, such as bringing 
asset replacements up to new standards through the I&M program, reducing outage risk 
through the vegetation management program, and the application of the standards to new 
construction.

To ensure resiliency prior to severe weather events, the Company needs to replace 
susceptible assets as they are identified.  The Company will continue to review stronger 
and lighter materials for consideration, and adopt new technologies and tools to improve 
its asset management techniques and develop innovative asset management and 
replacement strategies. 
Long-term, the benefits of the program will be widespread as more areas of the system are 
brought up to the storm-hardening construction standard.  The need to target specific 
feeders for storm-hardening upgrades should be reduced or eliminated as they are 
upgraded through other programs and projects.  Conversely, the storm-hardening 
construction standard may evolve to protect a longer list of sensitive equipment, such as 
smart capacitor banks or tie points to important customer-owned DG. 
Efforts focused on Survivability will also continue to drive improvements in areas where 
customers are most exposed to outages.   
29.5 Challenges: 
 
Some aging portions of the Company’s system could benefit from improved storm resiliency. 
However, the cost associated with hardening thousands of miles of overhead networks that are 
otherwise reliable is not justified on its own merits.  To ensure resiliency prior to severe weather 
events, the Company needs to identify and replace susceptible assets.  The Company will need to 
adopt new technologies and tools to improve its asset management techniques and develop 
innovative asset replacement strategies. Storm hardening can be implemented in numerous 
ways, with varying degrees of benefits. The installation of reinforced overhead lines, 
automated switching equipment, and accurate fault detection can reinforce reliability and 
shorten restoration time during high wind events or winter storms. In addition, circuit 
sectionalizing, additional of second supply lines or the addition of battery storage can 
provide alternate power supply to a subset of customers after a transmission outage.  All 
of these approaches can be utilized, with the related cost balanced against the residual 
reliability risk. In summary, there is no formal policy for climate mitigation for 
transmission assets, but through system assessments and current mitigation practices, 
the Company will be able to identify risk exposure.

Topic Catalog: 30. Substation Asset Management 
30.1 Introduction 
The Company’s robust planning, design, operations, and maintenance programs provide a high-
level of reliability to customers.  Asset management for substations plays a key role in achieving 
such highly reliable service.  The equipment purchased is carefully scrutinized and specifically 
chosen to provide the performance and longevity characteristics required for proper operation 
and protection of the system.  This equipment includes circuit breakers, transformers, 
switchgear, structures, and associated measurement and control devices.  The benefits of quality 
substation equipment extend to the distribution system downstream of the station.  Since 
substation equipment typically has expected service lives in excess of 50 years, it is critical to 
choose the right technology from reputable manufacturers.  It is also important that the 
manufacturers have a good track record for supporting their long-life products and making 
improvements that enhance reliability and satisfy the needs of an evolving electric system.
